options.B: Downward-sloping marginal physical product of labor curve
options.C: Downward-sloping long-run average total cost curve
options.D: Diseconomies of scale
options.E: Diminishing returns

text: Which of the following is a result of increasing returns to sale?

options.A: Upward-sloping short-run marginal cost curve
options.B: Downward-sloping marginal physical product of labor curve
options.C: Downward-sloping long-run average total cost curve
options.D: Diseconomies of scale
options.E: Diminishing returns

explanation: Increasing returns to scale means that doubling all inputs more than doubles output, so long-run average total cost falls as production expands, making the long-run average total cost curve slope downward. This is purely a long-run concept, so choices like diminishing returns or upward-sloping marginal cost are wrong because they describe short-run problems that occur when only some inputs are increased while others are held fixed.

text: Moving from left to right along a downwardsloping linear demand curve, price elasticity varies in which of the following ways?

options.A: First unit elastic, then inelastic throughout
options.B: First unit elastic, then elastic throughout
options.C: First inelastic, then unit elastic throughout
options.D: First elastic, then unit elastic, and finally inelastic
options.E: First inelastic, then unit elastic, and finally elastic

explanation: On a linear demand curve, the left side has a high price and low quantity, which creates a large price-to-quantity ratio and makes demand elastic, while the right side has a low price and high quantity, which creates a small ratio and makes demand inelastic, with unit elasticity at the midpoint. Many students mistakenly choose the reverse order because they confuse left-to-right movement with rising price rather than rising quantity. Since the slope is constant but the P/Q ratio steadily shrinks as you move down the curve, elasticity decreases from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.

text: At its current employment level of labor and capital, a firm observes the following. Marginal product of labor = 30 units Marginal product of capital = 60 units Price of labor = $3 per unit Price of capital = $15 per unit Which of the following actions should the firm take in order to achieve the least-cost combination of labor and capital and produce the same level of output? • • • • Labor Capital

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: Increase Decrease
options.C: Decrease Increase
options.D: Decrease Decrease

explanation: The firm should compare the marginal product per dollar for each input. Labor yields 10 units per dollar while capital yields only 4 units per dollar, so labor is more cost-effective. To produce the same output at lower cost, the firm should use more labor and less capital until the marginal product per dollar is equal across both inputs. A student might incorrectly choose to decrease labor and increase capital if they confuse the absolute marginal product with productivity per dollar spent.

text: If Lock chooses to charge the low price, the best course of action for Star would be to charge the

options.A: low price and earn a profit of $40
options.B: low price and earn a profit of $50
options.C: high price and earn a profit of $50
options.D: high price and earn a profit of $70

explanation: Because Lock has already chosen the low price, Star should pick the action that gives it the highest profit. Charging the low price earns Star $40, which is more than it would make by charging the high price. Option D is tempting because $70 is a larger amount, but that profit does not go to Star when Lock has chosen the low price.

text: One difference between a firm in a perfectly competitive market and an unregulated monopoly is that the

options.A: perfectly competitive firm can increase the quantity it sells at the market price, whereas the monopoly must lower its price to sell more
options.B: perfectly competitive firm sells differentiated products, whereas the monopoly sells a homogeneous product
options.C: price elasticity of demand for a monopoly is much higher than that for a perfectly competitive firm
options.D: monopolist seeks to maximize profits, whereas the perfectly competitive firm maximizes revenues
options.E: monopolist can never change a price, whereas the perfect competitor can

explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve, so it can sell more output without lowering the market price. In contrast, a monopoly faces the downward-sloping market demand curve and must decrease its price to sell additional units. Some students mistakenly think that only monopolies try to maximize profit and select option D, but both types of firms maximize profit by producing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

text: Assume that olive oil is produced in a constantcost, perfectly competitive industry, which is currently in long-run equilibrium. If the current price of olive oil is $5 per quart and the demand for olive oil increases, then the price of olive oil will change in which of the following ways in the short run and long run? Short Run Long Run

options.A: Be more than $5 Be more than $5
options.B: Be more than $5 Be equal to $5
options.C: Be equal to $5 Be equal to $5
options.D: Be less than $5 Be less than $5
options.E: Be less than $5 Be equal to $5

explanation: In the short run, the number of firms is fixed, so a rightward shift in demand pushes the market price above $5 and gives existing firms positive economic profit. Because the industry is perfectly competitive, that profit attracts new firms to enter in the long run, increasing supply until the price falls back to the minimum average total cost, which remains $5 in a constant-cost industry. Some students incorrectly choose A because they forget that free entry eliminates economic profit and restores the original price in the long run.

text: Which of the following is always true of a monopoly that is producing a level of output such that marginal revenue is negative?

options.A: It is experiencing economies of scale in production.
options.B: It is maximizing total revenue.
options.C: It is producing where demand is price elastic.
options.D: It could lower price to increase profits.
options.E: It could decrease output to increase profits.

explanation: If marginal revenue is negative, each additional unit sold actually reduces total revenue, which means the firm is operating on the inelastic portion of its demand curve. By decreasing output and raising its price, the monopoly would increase total revenue and also lower its total costs, so profits would rise. A tempting wrong answer is that it is maximizing total revenue, but total revenue is maximized only where marginal revenue equals zero, not where it is negative.

text: A cartel is difficult to maintain for which of the following reasons?

options.A: Consumers substitute away from the good when the price increases.
options.B: Individual cartel members are tempted to cheat on the agreement.
options.C: Although the total gain to cartel members is positive, all members lose when everyone sticks to the agreement.
options.D: Some firms will reduce output in an effort to lower costs of production.
options.E: Oligopolistic behavior is generally predictable.

explanation: Cartels are unstable because each member faces a strong temptation to cheat by producing more than its agreed-upon quota and selling at the high cartel price, which boosts individual profit. When enough firms do this, total supply rises, the market price falls, and the cartel agreement collapses. While option A describes a real response to higher prices, it reflects the law of demand rather than the internal incentive problem that actually destroys cartels.

text: Economists argue that most professional athletes earn economic rent because they

options.A: make additional income through commercial endorsements of products
options.B: are able to participate in sports for only a limited number of years before changing occupations
options.C: earn far more as professional athletes than they could earn in their next-best occupation
options.D: participate in sporting events only about six months during a year

explanation: Economic rent is the income a worker earns above the amount needed to keep them in their current job, measured as the gap between their actual pay and what they would earn in their next-best occupation. Because most professional athletes have rare talents, their salaries far exceed what they could make in other careers, so that large surplus is economic rent. Some students mistakenly think a short career creates rent, but economic rent is defined by the difference above opportunity cost, not by how long the career lasts.

text: For the firm shown in the graph above, which combination of output and price will maximize its profit? Output Price

options.A: it overproduces output and charges a price above marginal cost
options.B: it underproduces output and charges a price above marginal cost
options.C: it sometimes colludes with other firms to obtain higher prices
options.D: the price the monopolist charges is too low and it does not advertise
options.E: consumers must pay whatever price the monopolist charges

text: A monopolist is inefficient from society’s point of view because

options.A: it overproduces output and charges a price above marginal cost
options.B: it underproduces output and charges a price above marginal cost
options.C: it sometimes colludes with other firms to obtain higher prices
options.D: the price the monopolist charges is too low and it does not advertise
options.E: consumers must pay whatever price the monopolist charges

explanation: A monopolist restricts output below the socially efficient level, where price equals marginal cost, and instead charges a higher price that exceeds marginal cost. This creates deadweight loss because some mutually beneficial transactions do not occur. Option A is wrong because a monopolist underproduces, not overproduces, relative to the competitive outcome.

text: Suppose that at the current output level the marginal social cost of producing a good is greater than its marginal private cost, and that the marginal social benefit associated with production of the good is equal to its marginal private benefit. Which of the following government actions would most likely increase efficiency?

options.A: Taxing the production of the good
options.B: Taxing the production of substitute goods
options.C: Giving tax rebates to people who purchase the good
options.D: Subsidizing production of complementary goods
options.E: Subsidizing consumption of the good

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Because marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, producing this good creates a negative externality and the market supplies more than the socially optimal quantity. A tax on production increases producers' costs, shifting the supply curve leftward until output falls to the level where marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit. Subsidizing consumption or offering rebates would boost demand, which would worsen the overproduction and lower efficiency.

text: Suppose that in one week Sam can knit 5 sweaters or make 4 blankets and Rob can knit 10 sweaters or make 6 blankets. Which of the following is true?

options.A: Sam has an absolute advantage in making blankets.
options.B: Sam has an absolute advantage in knitting sweaters.
options.C: Sam has a comparative advantage in making blankets.
options.D: Sam has a comparative advantage in knitting sweaters.

explanation: Sam has a comparative advantage in making blankets because his opportunity cost is lower: he gives up 1.25 sweaters per blanket, while Rob gives up roughly 1.67 sweaters per blanket. Rob has an absolute advantage in both goods because he can produce more sweaters and more blankets in the same amount of time, so options A and B are wrong. Students often mistakenly choose D by confusing absolute and comparative advantage, but Sam's opportunity cost for one sweater is 0.8 blankets, which is actually higher than Rob's 0.6 blankets, giving Rob the comparative advantage in knitting sweaters.

text: If the market depicted in the diagram above is initially in equilibrium, which of the following will result from the government’s setting a price ceiling at ?

options.A: Quantity demanded will exceed quantity supplied.
options.B: Quantity supplied will exceed quantity demanded.
options.C: Market price will increase.
options.D: Market price will be unaffected.
options.E: Market price will decrease.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government

text: An increase in the supply of coffee could be caused by

options.A: a decrease in the price of cream, which is a complement to coffee
options.B: a decrease in the cost of labor used to produce coffee
options.C: an increase in consumer income
options.D: an increase in the demand for coffee
options.E: an increase in the price of coffee

explanation: A decrease in labor costs reduces production expenses, so coffee producers are willing to sell more at every price, shifting the supply curve to the right. A common mistake is choosing a higher coffee price, but that only increases the quantity supplied along the existing curve rather than shifting supply itself. Changes in consumer income or complement prices affect demand, not supply.

text: Which of the following explains why a decrease in the price of a normal good will lead to an increase in the quantity demanded of the good?

options.A: A lower price will increase consumers’ purchasing power.
options.B: A lower price will increase consumers’ marginal utility.
options.C: A lower price will increase demand for the good.
options.D: A lower price will increase demand for substitute goods.
options.E: A lower price will decrease demand for complementary goods.

explanation: A lower price raises consumers' real income, or purchasing power, which lets them buy more of a normal good—this is the income effect. Choice C is tempting but wrong because a price change causes a movement along the demand curve, which is called a change in quantity demanded, not a change in demand itself.

text: If SteveR Incorporated is a monopolistic producer of diamonds, the firm’s demand curve is downward sloping because

options.A: the number of diamonds SteveR Incorporated offers for sale affects the price of diamonds
options.B: marginal revenue is negative throughout the range of the demand curve
options.C: marginal revenue is positive throughout the range of the demand curve
options.D: the diamond industry consists of a few firms selling similar diamonds

explanation: As the only producer in the market, SteveR Incorporated must lower the price of diamonds in order to sell more output, which means the amount it offers for sale directly determines the market price. This control over price is exactly what gives a monopolist a downward-sloping demand curve. Choice D might seem appealing because diamonds are often associated with cartels, but it incorrectly describes an oligopoly rather than a single-firm monopoly, while choices B and C are wrong because marginal revenue is positive when demand is elastic and negative only when demand is inelastic.

text: Over the past 5 years, 50 new restaurants have opened and 30 have closed in the city of Zuni. Currently there are 110 restaurants operating in the city. Which of the following best represents the market structure, barriers to entry, and economic profits in the long run? Market Structure Barriers to Entry Long-Run Economic Profits

options.A: Perfect competition Low Negative
options.B: Perfect competition High Positive
options.C: Monopolistic competition Low Zero
options.D: Monopolistic competition High Positive
options.E: Monopolistic competition High Zero

explanation: Restaurants exemplify monopolistic competition because each serves a differentiated product in an industry with many independent firms. This type of market features low barriers to entry, which explains why new establishments can open easily and unprofitable ones can close. In the long run, that freedom of entry and exit pushes economic profits to zero. Many students mistakenly choose perfect competition, but because restaurant meals and dining experiences are not identical, monopolistic competition is the right fit.

text: For a perfectly competitive, increasing-cost industry, an increase in the industry’s demand will lead to which of the following in the long run?

options.A: An upward shift in each firm’s long-run average cost curve
options.B: An increase in each firm’s profit
options.C: A decrease in the price of an input and a decrease in total industry profits
options.D: A decrease in total industry sales
options.E: A decrease in total producer surplus and an increase in total consumer surplus

explanation: In an increasing-cost industry, greater industry output raises the prices of specialized inputs. As new firms enter in response to the demand increase, those higher input costs shift each firm’s long-run average cost curve upward. In the new long-run equilibrium each firm again earns zero economic profit, so the tempting idea that each firm’s profit rises is wrong.

text: If a good is available free of charge, an individual will consume it until

options.A: marginal utility is zero
options.B: average utility is zero
options.C: total utility is zero
options.D: marginal utility equals average utility
options.E: marginal utility equals total utility

explanation: When a good is free, the marginal cost of consuming another unit is zero, so a rational consumer will keep consuming as long as the extra satisfaction is positive. The individual stops exactly when marginal utility reaches zero, because beyond that point additional units would yield negative utility and reduce total satisfaction. Option D is tempting because it sets two utility measures equal, but marginal utility equals average utility only when average utility is at its maximum, not when consumption of a free good ends.

text: If a competitive firm pays its workers the value of the marginal product of the last worker hired, which of the following is true?

options.A: The firm will not earn any economic profits.
options.B: Workers will look for employment elsewhere.
options.C: The wage will be less than the marginal product.
options.D: The firm will not maximize profits.
options.E: The contribution of the last worker hired to the firm’s profit will be zero.

explanation: When a competitive firm pays a worker a wage equal to the value of that worker's marginal product, the revenue the last worker generates is exactly equal to the cost of hiring them. Therefore, the last worker adds zero to the firm's total profit, even though the firm is still maximizing profit overall. It is tempting to think this means the firm earns no economic profit, but that is not true because all previous workers hired had a marginal product value greater than the wage, contributing positively to the firm's bottom line.

text: Which of the following is necessary for a firm to practice price discrimination?

options.A: The government strictly enforces antitrust laws.
options.B: The firm is a member of a cartel.
options.C: The firm can prevent resale of its goods.
options.D: The demand curve for the product is perfectly inelastic.
options.E: The demand curve for the product is perfectly elastic.

explanation: A firm must be able to prevent resale to practice price discrimination, since otherwise consumers who bought at a low price could resell to those charged a high price and eliminate the price differences. It is tempting to think a perfectly inelastic demand curve is necessary, but the firm only needs market power and different willingness to pay across consumer groups. Antitrust enforcement and cartel membership have no bearing on the ability to charge different prices to different buyers.

text: A monopolistically competitive firm’s demand curve will be highly elastic if which of the following exists?

options.A: A high degree of product differentiation
options.B: A highly elastic supply curve for the firm
options.C: High barriers to entry in this industry
options.D: A high degree of product substitutability
options.E: A small number of competitors

explanation: When consumers view the products of competing firms as close substitutes, they will readily switch to a rival if one firm raises its price, which makes the firm's demand curve highly elastic. A tempting wrong choice is product differentiation, but a high degree of differentiation actually means fewer close substitutes exist, so consumers are less responsive to price changes and demand becomes more inelastic. Therefore, substitutability, not differentiation, creates the elastic demand.

text: Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.5, and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.3. Which of the following statements is definitely true?

options.A: Country A has higher average income than Country B.
options.B: Country B has higher average income than Country A.
options.C: Income is more evenly distributed in Country A than in Country B.
options.D: Income is more evenly distributed in Country B than in Country A.
options.E: Country A has more deadweight loss than Country B.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale from 0 to 1, where a lower value means income is distributed more equally among the population. Since Country B's coefficient of 0.3 is lower than Country A's 0.5, income is definitely more evenly distributed in Country B. Choices A and B are incorrect because the Gini coefficient says nothing about a country's average income or total wealth, only about how income is shared within each country.

text: If labor is the only variable input of a firm and the marginal product of labor is falling, the firm will always produce

options.A: more than the profit-maximizing level of output
options.B: less than the profit-maximizing level of output
options.C: at a level of output where average total cost is at a minimum
options.D: at a level of output where marginal costs are rising

explanation: Because labor is the only variable input, marginal cost equals the wage divided by the marginal product of labor. Therefore, when the marginal product of labor is falling, marginal cost must be rising, meaning the firm produces where marginal costs are increasing. It is tempting to choose A or B because diminishing returns might seem like a mistake, but firms usually maximize profit in this range, not above or below it.

text: The graph above shows the conditions that a monopsonist faces in a labor market. How many workers would this monopsonist hire and what wage rate would it pay? Number of Workers Wage Rate
explanation: A monopsonist in a labor market hires workers where the marginal factor cost (MFC) equals the marginal revenue product (MRP), which is represented by the demand curve. In the graph, this occurs at 10 workers. The wage rate is determined by the supply curve at that quantity, which is $30. The answer choice C correctly identifies 10 workers and $30 as the wage rate. Choice A is incorrect because it uses the wage from the demand curve, which is not what the monopsonist pays.

text: Public goods are underproduced in a competitive market because the free-rider problem causes which of the following?

options.A: Fixed supply
options.B: Effective price ceilings
options.C: Reduced market demand
options.D: Negative externalities

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The free-rider problem leads consumers to hide their true willingness to pay since they can enjoy the benefit without contributing, which causes the market demand curve to be lower than the true social demand. With demand understated, producers lack the profit incentive to supply the socially optimal quantity. A tempting wrong answer is negative externalities, but those involve harmful side effects that cause overproduction of private goods, not the underproduction of public goods caused by non-excludability.

text: Improvements in technology for producing all goods must result in

options.A: an inward shift in the production possibilities curve
options.B: an outward shift in the production possibilities curve
options.C: a flatter production possibilities curve
options.D: a steeper production possibilities curve
options.E: greater unemployment of labor

explanation: When technology improves for all goods, the economy can produce more of everything, so the production possibilities curve shifts outward. A change in the curve's slope would require opportunity costs to shift in a specific way, which is not guaranteed here. Greater unemployment would move production inside the curve rather than shift the curve itself.

text: The quantity of peanuts supplied increased from 40 tons per week to 60 tons per week when the price of peanuts increased from $4 per ton to $5 per ton. The price elasticity of supply for peanuts over this price range is

options.A: elastic
options.B: inelastic
options.C: unit elastic
options.D: perfectly elastic
options.E: perfectly inelastic

explanation: Using the midpoint formula, quantity supplied rises by 40 percent while price rises by about 22 percent, giving a price elasticity of supply of roughly 1.8. Because that value is greater than one, supply is elastic over this range. Students often mistakenly pick inelastic because the price change seems small in absolute terms, but elasticity depends on percentage changes, not dollar amounts.

text: Which of the following best describes the law of demand?

options.A: The price of a good increases when the demand for the good increases.
options.B: The price of a good decreases when the supply of the good decreases.
options.C: When the price of a good increases, its demand decreases.
options.D: When the price of a good decreases, its quantity demanded increases.
options.E: Demand creates its own supply.

explanation: The law of demand states that, all else equal, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so a lower price leads consumers to buy more of a good. Choice D captures this exact relationship. Choice C is tempting but incorrect because it says "demand" rather than "quantity demanded"—a change in price changes how much people are willing and able to buy along the curve, but it does not shift the entire demand curve itself.

text: Assume that ice cream is a normal good. If the price of ice cream decreases, the substitution effect and the income effect will lead to which of the following changes in ice cream consumption? Substitution Effect Income Effect

options.A: Increase Decrease
options.B: Increase Increase
options.C: Increase No change
options.D: Decrease Increase
options.E: Decrease No change

explanation: When the price of ice cream falls, the substitution effect leads consumers to buy more because it is now relatively cheaper than other goods. Because ice cream is a normal good, the income effect also increases consumption, since the lower price effectively raises consumers' real income and they purchase more of the good. A tempting wrong choice shows the income effect decreasing consumption, which is only true for an inferior good, not a normal good.

text: Short-run marginal costs eventually increase because of the effects of

options.A: increasing marginal product
options.B: diminishing marginal product
options.C: diseconomies of scale
options.D: economies of scale
options.E: increasing fixed costs

explanation: Adding more variable inputs like labor to fixed capital eventually causes diminishing marginal product, where each additional worker adds less to total output than the previous one. Since each new input produces fewer units of output, the cost of producing one more unit naturally rises. Diseconomies of scale might seem related, but that concept applies only to the long run when all inputs can be changed, so it does not explain this short-run behavior.

text: If a government eliminated an effective price floor in a market, all of the following would occur EXCEPT:

options.A: The surplus would be eliminated.
options.B: The price would decrease.
options.C: The quantity supplied would decrease.
options.D: The quantity demanded would increase.
options.E: The supply of the good would increase.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Eliminating an effective price floor allows the price to fall back to equilibrium, which eliminates the surplus, decreases quantity supplied, and increases quantity demanded. However, removing the price floor does not shift the supply curve itself; it only causes a movement along the existing supply curve. Students often confuse the decrease in quantity supplied with an increase in supply, but supply only changes when the underlying conditions of production change, not when a price control is removed.

text: Which of the following must be true if a firm is experiencing economies of scale?

options.A: All costs are explicit.
options.B: Long-run average total cost decreases as the firm’s output increases.
options.C: Economic profits decrease as the firm’s output increases.
options.D: Long-run average total cost remains constant as the firm’s output decreases.
options.E: Proportionate increases in inputs result in less-than-proportionate increases in output.

explanation: Economies of scale occur when a firm’s long-run average total cost falls as its output increases, which is exactly what option B states. This happens because the firm can spread its fixed costs across more units or gain from worker specialization. Option E is a common distractor because it describes decreasing returns to scale, where proportionate input increases yield smaller output gains and per-unit costs actually rise.

text: Compared to a perfectly competitive industry with the same demand and cost curves, a monopoly’s price and output will be which of the following? Price Output

options.A: The same Higher
options.B: Higher The same
options.C: Higher Lower
options.D: Lower The same
options.E: Lower Higher

explanation: A monopoly produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and because its marginal revenue curve lies below the downward-sloping demand curve, it restricts output to a level below the perfectly competitive equilibrium where price equals marginal cost. The monopoly then charges the higher price consumers are willing to pay for that smaller quantity on the demand curve. Option B is tempting because students often think monopolies simply raise prices without cutting output, but profit maximization requires reducing quantity to push price up along the demand curve.

text: If the demand for a good is perfectly price inelastic in the short run and the supply curve is upward sloping, imposing a sales tax on the good will

options.A: leave the price paid by consumers unchanged
options.B: decrease the after-tax revenues received by suppliers
options.C: increase the after-tax revenues received by suppliers
options.D: not change the after-tax revenues received by suppliers
options.E: not change the total expenditures by consumers on the good

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Because demand is perfectly inelastic, the quantity traded does not change when a tax is imposed, and the entire burden falls on consumers in the form of a higher price. Since suppliers continue to receive the same net price and sell the same amount, their after-tax revenue remains unchanged. Choice B is tempting because taxes often reduce the net price received by sellers, but that outcome requires the tax to lower the equilibrium quantity, which cannot happen when demand is perfectly inelastic.

text: The characteristic of oligopolistic firms that makes them different from all other types of firms is that oligopolistic firms

options.A: are regulated by a state agency or federal agency
options.B: consider each other’s decisions
options.C: advertise their products
options.D: produce differentiated products
options.E: produce identical products

explanation: The key feature that distinguishes oligopoly from all other market structures is strategic interdependence, which means each firm must consider how its rivals will respond to its decisions about price or output. This mutual interdependence does not exist in perfect competition, monopoly, or monopolistic competition. Choices like product differentiation or advertising may occur in oligopolies, but they are also common in other market structures, so they are not the defining difference.

text: For the firm shown in the graph above, the shortrun, profit-maximizing strategy would be to set output at

options.A: Q1, price at P1, and suffer a loss
options.B: Q1, price at P3, and earn an economic profit
options.C: Q1, price at P3, and earn only a normal profit
options.D: Q2, price at P2, and earn an economic profit
options.E: Q2, price at P2, and earn only a normal profit

explanation: In the short run, a firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC). The graph shows that MR and MC intersect at output Q2. At this output level, the price is determined by the demand curve, which is P2. Since the price (P2) equals the average total cost (ATC) at Q2, the firm earns only a normal profit, not an economic profit or loss. Option D is incorrect because while the output is correct, the firm would earn an economic profit if price were above ATC, which it is not at Q2.

text: Which of the following will tend to make the demand for a product more elastic?

options.A: New firms which produce similar products enter the industry.
options.B: A change in taste and preferences makes the product more desirable.
options.C: The product is necessary for use with a complement.
options.D: Production of the product is protected by a patent.
options.E: Production cost of the product decreases.

explanation: When new firms enter with similar products, consumers gain more substitutes, making them more sensitive to price changes and increasing demand elasticity. A decrease in production costs might seem relevant, but it shifts the supply curve rather than changing how responsive buyers are to price. With more available alternatives, consumers can easily switch away if the price rises, which directly makes demand more elastic.

text: In a perfectly competitive labor market, an increase in an effective minimum wage will result in

options.A: an increase in the supply of workers
options.B: a decrease in the supply of workers
options.C: a decrease in the demand for workers
options.D: more workers being hired
options.E: fewer workers being hired

explanation: An effective minimum wage is a binding price floor set above the equilibrium wage, so firms respond by moving up along their labor demand curve and reducing employment. This means fewer workers are actually hired, creating a surplus of labor. A common wrong choice is C, but the minimum wage changes the quantity of labor demanded, not the demand curve itself.

text: Which of the following taxes contributes most to decreasing inequality in the distribution of income?

options.A: Progressive income taxes
options.B: Sales taxes
options.C: Proportional income taxes
options.D: Excise taxes
options.E: Import tariffs on necessities

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Progressive income taxes require higher-income households to pay a larger percentage of their income in taxes than lower-income households, which directly narrows the gap between rich and poor after-tax incomes. Sales taxes might appear fair because everyone pays the same rate at the register, but they are regressive since lower-income families spend a greater share of their earnings on taxed goods, so these taxes actually widen inequality.

text: A free-rider problem arises when a good is

options.A: nonrival
options.B: nondepletable
options.C: nonexcludable
options.D: produced in a competitive market
options.E: produced in a monopolistic market

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The free-rider problem occurs because people can benefit from a good without paying for it when they cannot be prevented from using it. This happens when a good is nonexcludable, meaning the supplier cannot easily exclude those who do not pay. Many students incorrectly choose nonrival because public goods are both nonrival and nonexcludable, but nonrivalry alone does not cause free riding since the supplier could still charge admission if the good were excludable.

text: According to the production possibilities curve above, which of the following is true?

options.A: The opportunity cost of producing another unit of good Y in terms of good X increases as more of good Y is produced.
options.B: The opportunity cost of producing another unit of good Y in terms of good X decreases as more of good Y is produced.
options.C: The opportunity cost of producing another unit of good X in terms of good Y increases as more of good X is produced.
options.D: The opportunity cost of producing another unit of good X in terms of good Y decreases as more of good X is produced.
options.E: The opportunity cost of producing another unit of either good remains constant as the production of the other good increases.

text: Which of the following is true in a capitalist economy?

options.A: The factors of production are collectively owned.
options.B: The factors of production are distributed according to needs.
options.C: The prices of goods and services are usually determined by the government.
options.D: The prices of goods and services are set so that an equitable distribution of private property is achieved.
options.E: Prices serve as incentives for factors of production to move to the markets where they are most valued.

explanation: In a capitalist economy, prices act as signals that guide resources to their most productive and valued uses, giving producers and workers a reason to shift toward markets offering higher returns. This decentralized price mechanism is a defining feature of market capitalism. A common wrong choice like A is incorrect because collective ownership of the factors of production describes a socialist or command system, not a private market economy.

text: A city transit authority increases the price of subway and bus tickets from $1.25 to $1.50. If the demand for these tickets is price inelastic, the number of people riding buses and subways and the city’s revenues will most likely change in which of the following ways? Number of People Riding City’s Revenues

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: Decrease Increase
options.C: Decrease Decrease
options.D: Decrease Remain constant
options.E: Remain constant Increase

explanation: When the ticket price rises, the law of demand means fewer people will ride, though the decrease is relatively small because demand is price inelastic. Since the percentage drop in ridership is smaller than the percentage increase in price, total revenue increases. A common mistake is assuming inelastic demand means quantity demanded does not change at all, but it still falls—just by a smaller proportion than the price rise.

text: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay for units of a good and the price consumers actually pay for units of the good is called

options.A: marginal utility
options.B: producer surplus
options.C: consumer surplus
options.D: economic rent

explanation: Consumer surplus represents the extra value buyers receive when they pay less than the highest price they would have been willing to pay. You can think of it as the area below the demand curve and above the market price. Producer surplus is easy to confuse with this, but it measures the benefit to sellers when they receive a price above their lowest acceptable price, not the benefit to buyers.

text: Which of the following is true if consuming one unit of a good yields 100 utils and consuming the second unit of the good increases satisfaction by 20 utils?

options.A: The marginal utility of the first unit is 20.
options.B: The marginal utility of the second unit is 80.
options.C: The marginal utility of the second unit is 120.
options.D: The total utility of consuming two units is 120.
options.E: The total utility of consuming one unit is greater than the total utility of consuming two units.

explanation: Total utility is the sum of all satisfaction, so 100 utils from the first unit plus 20 additional utils from the second equals 120 utils after two units. The second unit’s marginal utility is 20, not 80, because marginal utility measures only the extra satisfaction from that additional unit. Therefore, choice D is correct, while choice B is tempting only if you incorrectly subtract the second unit’s gain from the first unit’s total.

text: If a new tax on capital increases a firm’s fixed cost of production, which of the following will occur in the short run?

options.A: Marginal cost will increase.
options.B: Average variable cost will increase.
options.C: Average total cost will increase.
options.D: The profit-maximizing level of output will increase.
options.E: The profit-maximizing level of output will decrease. • The marginal product of labor equals 250 units of output. • The marginal product of capital equals 750 units of output. • The price of labor is $50 per person. • The price of capital is $100 per unit.

explanation: Average total cost includes average fixed cost, so when a tax raises fixed costs, ATC shifts upward. Marginal cost and average variable cost are unaffected because they depend on variable inputs, not fixed expenses. A common mistake is thinking the profit-maximizing output changes, but since the MC curve does not shift, the firm still produces where marginal revenue equals the same marginal cost as before.

text: Given the information above, which of the following is true for a firm buying its labor and capital inputs in a perfectly competitive market?

options.A: The firm is producing its current level of output with the least-cost combination of labor and capital.
options.B: The firm is maximizing profits with its current combination of inputs.
options.C: The firm’s level of output will remain the same if 1 unit of capital is substituted for 2 units of labor.
options.D: The firm’s input costs will decrease if 2 units of labor are substituted for 1 unit of capital.
options.E: The firm can reduce the cost of its current level of output by laying off workers and employing more capital.

text: At 100 units of output, a firm’s total cost is $10,000. If the firm’s total fixed cost is $4,000, its average variable cost is equal to
Which of the following statements correctly identifies a difference between perfect competition and monopolistic competition?

options.A: In perfect competition there are no barriers to entry, but there are strong barriers in monopolistic competition.
options.B: In perfect competition there are many firms, but in monopolistic competition there are only a few firms.
options.C: In perfect competition the firms all sell products that are exactly the same, but in monopolistic competition each firm sells a slightly differentiated product.
options.D: In perfect competition firms maximize profit by selling the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, but in monopolistic competition firms maximize profit by selling the quantity where marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.
options.E: In perfect competition there are few consumers, but in monopolistic competition there are many consumers.

explanation: The defining difference between these market structures is that perfectly competitive firms sell identical, standardized products, while monopolistically competitive firms sell slightly differentiated products, which gives each firm a small degree of market power. It is tempting to think choice A is correct because the name sounds like monopoly, but monopolistic competition actually has low barriers to entry, just like perfect competition. Choice D is also incorrect because all profit-maximizing firms, regardless of market structure, produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

text: The most profitable level of output for any firm operating in the short run is the level of output at which

options.A: marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost by the highest amount
options.B: marginal revenue equals marginal cost
options.C: price exceeds average cost by the highest amount
options.D: price equals average cost

explanation: A firm maximizes profit by producing every unit that adds more to revenue than to cost, so it should keep expanding output until marginal revenue equals marginal cost. If marginal revenue were greater than marginal cost, producing another unit would increase total profit, meaning stopping earlier would leave money on the table. Option A is tempting because a large gap sounds beneficial, but profit actually rises as long as marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, making the equality point the true peak.

text: For an unregulated monopolist, the profitmaximizing quantity will always be

options.A: in the elastic region of the demand curve
options.B: where marginal revenue equals price
options.C: where price equals average total cost
options.D: where price equals marginal cost
options.E: where the marginal cost curve intersects the demand curve

explanation: A monopolist maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and since marginal revenue is positive only when demand is elastic, the profit-maximizing quantity must always lie in the elastic region of the demand curve. If the firm produced in the inelastic region, marginal revenue would be negative while marginal cost is positive, so cutting output would increase profit. A tempting wrong choice is where price equals marginal cost, but that describes the efficient outcome in perfect competition, not the profit-maximizing behavior of a monopolist.

text: If a per-unit tax is imposed on a monopolist, how will the monopolist’s marginal cost curve, output, and the price paid by consumers be affected? Marginal Cost Output Price

options.A: Shift down Increase Decrease
options.B: Shift down Decrease Decrease
options.C: No shift Decrease Decrease
options.D: Shift up Decrease Increase
options.E: Shift up Increase Increase

explanation: A per-unit tax increases the cost of producing each additional unit, which shifts the monopolist's marginal cost curve upward. Because the monopolist chooses the output level where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, the higher marginal cost leads to a lower profit-maximizing quantity and a higher price along the demand curve. Choice E is tempting because it correctly identifies that the marginal cost curve shifts up and price rises, but it wrongly suggests output increases when a monopolist actually cuts production in response to higher costs.

text: The demand curve for labor for a monopolist that faces a perfectly competitive factor market is called the

options.A: average product curve
options.B: marginal product curve
options.C: marginal revenue curve
options.D: marginal revenue product curve
options.E: value of the average product curve Number of Workers Parts per Week 0 0 1 100 2 190 3 270 4 340 5 400 6 450 7

explanation: The demand for labor is the marginal revenue product curve because each additional worker generates revenue equal to their marginal product multiplied by the firm's marginal revenue. A monopolist in a competitive factor market hires workers up to the point where this MRP equals the market wage. Do not confuse this with the marginal revenue curve, which measures extra revenue from selling another unit of output rather than from hiring another worker.

text: The table above describes the production function of an auto parts manufacturer. Assume that the firm can hire as many workers as it wants at the market wage rate of $600 per week per worker and sell as many auto parts as it wants at the price of $10 per part. To maximize profits, the firm should hire

options.A: 0 workers
options.B: 1 worker
options.C: 3 workers
options.D: 5 workers
options.E: 7 workers

explanation: To maximize profit, the firm should hire workers up to the point where the value of the marginal product (VMP) equals the wage. The VMP is calculated as the marginal product (MP) of labor multiplied by the price of the output. The price is $10 per part. The marginal product of the 3rd worker is 80 parts (270 - 190), so the VMP is $800. The wage is $600, so hiring the 3rd worker is profitable. The marginal product of the 4th worker is 70 parts (340 - 270), so the VMP is $700, which is still greater than the wage. The marginal product of the 5th worker is 60 parts (400 - 340), so the VMP is $600, which equals the wage. The marginal product of the 6th worker is 50 parts (450 - 400), so the VMP is $500, which is less than the wage. Therefore, the firm should hire 5 workers. However, the official answer is C, which is 3 workers. This suggests that the firm should hire up to the point where the VMP is greater than or equal to the wage, but the correct answer should be 5 workers. The official answer key may be incorrect.

text: Monopolistically competitive firms are considered inefficient in allocating society’s resources for which of the following reasons?

options.A: In equilibrium, the marginal benefit exceeds the price charged by the firms.
options.B: In equilibrium, the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost of production.
options.C: In equilibrium, the marginal revenue of the firm is not equal to its marginal cost.
options.D: In long-run equilibrium, the firm is earning economic profits.

explanation: In monopolistic competition, firms maximize profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, but they set price above marginal cost because they face downward-sloping demand curves. Since the price consumers pay represents the marginal benefit of the good, having marginal benefit exceed marginal cost means society values additional units more than the cost of producing them, resulting in an underallocation of resources. Option D is incorrect because free entry and exit eliminate economic profits in the long run, leaving firms with only normal profits.

text: As a factor of production, capital refers to the

options.A: money available to start a business
options.B: stocks and bonds issued by businesses to raise funds
options.C: financial investment of businesses
options.D: currency in circulation and deposits in financial institutions
options.E: tools and machinery used to produce goods and services

explanation: In economics, capital as a factor of production means physical capital—tools, machinery, and equipment used to make goods and services. This is different from financial capital, which is money or assets used to fund a business. Many students incorrectly choose answers involving money or stocks because in everyday language "capital" often means cash, but in microeconomics it specifically refers to physical productive resources.

text: Which of the following will cause the supply curve for shoes to shift to the right?

options.A: An increase in the price of socks, assuming that shoes and socks are complements
options.B: A decrease in the price of sandals, assuming that shoes and sandals are substitutes
options.C: An increase in the wages of shoe workers
options.D: An increase in the number of firms producing shoes
options.E: A decrease in the income of consumers, assuming that shoes are normal goods

explanation: An increase in the number of firms producing shoes adds more sellers to the market, which increases the quantity supplied at every price and shifts the supply curve to the right. A common wrong choice is an increase in workers' wages, but that raises production costs and would actually decrease supply by shifting the curve to the left. Remember that changes in the number of sellers directly shift supply, while factors like income or prices of related goods shift demand instead.

text: The diagram above depicts demand and supply curves in a city’s rental housing market. If a price ceiling of $1,000 is imposed on the market, which of the following will occur?

options.A: There will be a surplus of rental housing in the city.
options.B: The demand curve for housing will shift to the right.
options.C: The supply curve for housing will shift to the right.
options.D: The quantity of rental housing supplied will decrease.
options.E: The quantity of rental housing demanded will increase.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The diagram shows a supply and demand graph for rental housing with a price ceiling of $1,000 imposed below the equilibrium price of $2,000. A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, meaning quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. At the $1,000 price, the quantity supplied is determined by the supply curve at that price, which is lower than the equilibrium quantity, so the quantity supplied decreases. Option E is tempting because demand increases at lower prices, but the question asks what will occur, and the most direct and correct outcome is the decrease in quantity supplied. Option A is wrong because a shortage, not a surplus, occurs. Options B and C are wrong because a price ceiling does not shift the demand or supply curves.

text: For consumers, assume that fish sticks and tacos are substitutes. Which of the following graphs illustrates the effect on the taco market if the price of fish sticks increases?

options.A: below P1
options.B: between P1 and P2
options.C: below P2
options.D: between P2 and P3
options.E: between P3 and P4

text: In the short run, the firm will realize an economic loss but will continue to produce if the price is

options.A: below P1
options.B: between P1 and P2
options.C: below P2
options.D: between P2 and P3
options.E: between P3 and P4

explanation: In the short run, a firm produces despite an economic loss as long as price is high enough to cover average variable cost, since it can pay part of its fixed costs. That range is above the shutdown price but below the break-even price, which corresponds to option B. Option C is tempting because any price below average total cost yields a loss, but it is incorrect because it includes prices too low to cover variable costs, at which point the firm would shut down.

text: Which of the following MUST be true in the long run?

options.A: The equilibrium price will be P2, since that is where marginal cost equals minimum average variable cost.
options.B: The equilibrium price will be above P3, since firms must make an economic profit to stay in business.
options.C: If the price is above P2, new firms will enter the industry.
options.D: If the price is above P3, new firms will enter the industry.
options.E: If the price is above P4, firms will exit the industry.

explanation: In a perfectly competitive market, new firms enter in the long run whenever the market price exceeds the minimum average total cost, because existing firms are earning positive economic profits. Option C correctly captures this entry condition by stating that a price above this long-run equilibrium threshold attracts new competitors. Option A is tempting because it points to a cost curve intersection, but it wrongly claims long-run equilibrium occurs where marginal cost equals minimum average variable cost, which is actually the short-run shutdown point rather than the break-even point.

text: Which of the following MUST be true of the long run?

options.A: It is at least one year in duration.
options.B: All factors of production are variable.
options.C: At least one factor of production is fixed.
options.D: Marginal costs are constant.
options.E: Average total costs are constant.

explanation: The long run is defined by the fact that all factors of production are variable, so firms can change any input including capital and plant size. This is different from the short run, where at least one factor is fixed. Choice A is incorrect because economists define the long run by input flexibility, not by a specific time period such as one year.

text: In order for a firm to engage in price discrimination, it must be

options.A: able to separate consumers into different groups based on demand elasticities
options.B: producing in the inelastic portion of its demand curve to raise its price and increase total revenue
options.C: a price taker
options.D: experiencing economies of scale in the relevant range of production
options.E: experiencing constant marginal cost

explanation: A firm can only price discriminate if it can divide consumers into distinct groups with different demand elasticities and prevent resale between them, allowing it to charge each group a different price. Option C is wrong because a price taker lacks market power entirely and must accept the going market price, making any form of price discrimination impossible.

text: Which of the following market structures results in allocative efficiency?

options.A: Monopoly
options.B: Monopolistic competition
options.C: Perfect competition
options.D: Natural monopoly

explanation: Perfect competition achieves allocative efficiency because firms produce where price equals marginal cost, ensuring that resources are allocated to the goods society values most. A monopoly might seem efficient because it can produce at a large scale, but it charges a price above marginal cost, which prevents allocative efficiency and creates deadweight loss.

text: The following table shows the profits associated with the pricing strategies of two oligopolistic firms, Agronomia and Farmingdale. Each firm has two possible strategies: to charge a low price or a high price. The first entry in each cell shows the profits to Agronomia and the second the profits to Farmingdale. Farmingdale charges high price. Farmingdale charges low price. Agronomia charges high price. $150, $150 $50, $300 Agronomia charges low price. $300, $50 $100, $100 If the two firms do not cooperate, as a result of the firms’ pricing decisions the profits of each firm will be which of the following? Agronomia’s Profit Farmingdale’s Profit
explanation: Each firm has a dominant strategy to charge a low price because doing so always earns it more profit no matter what the other firm chooses. When both firms act independently, they reach a Nash equilibrium where both charge low prices and each earns $100. Option B is tempting because mutual high pricing would yield $150 each, but without cooperation either firm could gain by secretly cutting its price, making that outcome unstable.

text: Which of the following will occur in a perfectly competitive labor market if Firm X’s demand for labor decreases? Equilibrium Market Wage Rate Employment by Firm X

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: No change No change
options.C: No change Decrease
options.D: Decrease Decrease
options.E: Decrease No change

explanation: In a perfectly competitive labor market, a single firm is a wage taker, so Firm X cannot influence the market wage. When Firm X’s demand for labor falls, it simply hires fewer workers at the existing market wage, causing its employment to decrease while the equilibrium wage stays the same. Students often incorrectly choose D because they confuse a single firm’s demand decrease with a market-wide demand decrease, which would lower the wage.

text: The graph above shows the marginal revenue product (MRP) and the market wage rate for a profit-maximizing firm. Which of the following is true of the firm’s hiring of labor?

options.A: It should hire 15 workers.
options.B: It should hire between 15 and 40 workers.
options.C: It should hire 40 workers.
options.D: It should hire between 40 and 90 workers.
options.E: It should hire 90 workers.

explanation: A profit-maximizing firm hires workers up to the point where the marginal revenue product (MRP) of labor equals the market wage rate. In the graph, the MRP curve intersects the horizontal market wage line at 40 workers. Therefore, the firm should hire 40 workers. Option A is incorrect because hiring only 15 workers would mean the firm is not maximizing profit, as MRP is still greater than the wage. Option E is incorrect because hiring 90 workers would mean MRP is less than the wage, which would reduce profit.

text: Which of the following best defines a pure public good?

options.A: A good that is provided free of charge to the public
options.B: A good that is provided by the government, whether or not a fee is charged
options.C: A good that is efficiently produced only by a monopoly
options.D: A good whose benefits can be enjoyed by many consumers at the same time and from which consumers cannot be excluded
options.E: A good that by law must be available to all consumers without discrimination on the basis of sex, race, or religion

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: A pure public good is characterized by non-rivalry, meaning many people can consume it simultaneously without diminishing its availability, and non-excludability, meaning consumers cannot be prevented from using it. Option D correctly captures both defining features. Many students mistakenly select A or B because they confuse public goods with free or government-provided goods, but the economic definition depends solely on these consumption properties, not on price or provider.

text: A perfectly competitive manufacturing industry pollutes public water in its production process, leaving the water unsuitable for use by the surrounding communities. At the market equilibrium output level, which of the following is true?

options.A: Marginal private cost exceeds marginal social cost.
options.B: Marginal private cost exceeds marginal private benefit.
options.C: Marginal social cost exceeds marginal social benefit.
options.D: The market equilibrium output is equal to the socially efficient output.
options.E: The market equilibrium output is less than the socially efficient output.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Because the industry pollutes, the marginal social cost of production is greater than the marginal private cost. At the market equilibrium, firms produce where marginal private cost equals marginal private benefit, so marginal social cost exceeds marginal social benefit since the harm to the community is not reflected in market prices. A common mistake is thinking the market underproduces, but with this negative externality the market actually overproduces compared to the socially efficient level.

text: Assume that under new environmental regulations, tire companies have to pay taxes based on how much pollution is created when producing each tire. The price paid by consumers and the quantity of tires sold will most likely change in which of the following ways? Price Quantity

options.A: Increase Decrease
options.B: Increase Increase
options.C: Decrease Increase
options.D: Decrease Decrease

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The tax raises producers' costs, shifting the supply curve leftward. This leads to a higher equilibrium price and a lower equilibrium quantity. A common mistake is choosing an option with an increase in quantity because of confusing a tax with a subsidy.

text: The market for goldfish is perfectly competitive. From year 1 to year 2, both the price and the quantity of goldfish sold increase. This is most likely caused by

options.A: an increase in the supply
options.B: a decrease in the supply
options.C: an increase in the demand
options.D: a decrease in the demand
options.E: a decrease in both the demand and the supply

explanation: An increase in demand shifts the demand curve rightward, causing both the equilibrium price and the quantity sold to rise. A common wrong choice is an increase in supply, which would raise quantity but lower price rather than increase it.

text: Using the same amount of time and resources, Jack can assemble either 10 bikes or 5 computers, whereas Sam can assemble either 5 bikes or 5 computers. Based on the data, which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Sam has an absolute advantage in assembling bikes.
options.B: Sam has an absolute advantage in assembling computers.
options.C: Sam has a comparative advantage in assembling bikes.
options.D: Jack has a comparative advantage in assembling bikes.
options.E: Jack has a comparative advantage in assembling both bikes and computers.

explanation: Jack gives up only half a computer to assemble one bike, while Sam gives up a whole computer, so Jack has the lower opportunity cost and the comparative advantage in bikes. Sam actually has the comparative advantage in computers because his opportunity cost there is lower. Choice E is tempting because Jack produces more bikes and an equal number of computers, but absolute advantage does not determine comparative advantage, and one person cannot have the comparative advantage in both goods.

text: Given an increase in the price of material K— which is an input used to produce good X—and an increase in the price of good Y—which is a substitute for good X—which of the following will definitely occur?

options.A: The equilibrium price of good X will decrease.
options.B: The equilibrium price of good X will increase.
options.C: The equilibrium quantity of good X will be unaffected.
options.D: The equilibrium quantity of good X will increase.
options.E: The equilibrium quantity of good X will decrease.

explanation: An increase in the cost of material K reduces the supply of good X, shifting the supply curve to the left, while a higher price for substitute good Y leads consumers to buy more X, shifting the demand curve to the right. Both of these shifts push the equilibrium price upward, so the price of X will definitely increase. The effect on equilibrium quantity is uncertain because the supply decrease lowers quantity while the demand increase raises it, which makes it tempting to think quantity will fall, but that is not guaranteed.

text: An entrepreneur has earned enough total revenue to cover her accounting costs, but economic losses are being incurred. What must be true?

options.A: Her accounting costs are larger than her economic costs.
options.B: Her accounting profits are less than her implicit costs.
options.C: Her accounting profits are greater than her economic costs.
options.D: Her economic losses are less than her total fixed costs.
options.E: Her implicit costs are less than her accounting costs.

explanation: Accounting profit is total revenue minus explicit costs, and economic profit is accounting profit minus implicit costs. Since her revenue covers all accounting costs, accounting profit is at least zero, but an economic loss means that same accounting profit is not large enough to cover her implicit costs—so accounting profit must be less than implicit costs. A tempting wrong choice is (E), but implicit costs do not have to be smaller than accounting costs; they only need to exceed the firm’s accounting profit to produce an economic loss.

text: If nations specialize according to their comparative advantage and engage in international trade with each other, each nation can

options.A: produce outside its production possibilities curve
options.B: consume outside its production possibilities curve
options.C: shift its production possibilities curve to the right
options.D: become more self-sufficient
options.E: produce more of all goods

explanation: Specialization and trade allow countries to consume combinations of goods that lie beyond their own production possibilities curve because they can import goods they do not produce efficiently. While a nation still cannot produce outside its PPC since its resources and technology are unchanged, trade effectively expands its consumption options. Many students incorrectly choose A, but trade affects consumption possibilities rather than production capacity.

text: When total physical product is at its maximum, marginal physical product must be

options.A: greater than one
options.B: equal to one
options.C: equal to zero
options.D: less than zero

explanation: Marginal physical product is the additional output produced by one more unit of input, so when total physical product stops increasing and reaches its peak, that additional output must be exactly zero. If marginal product were positive, total product would still be rising, and if it were negative, total product would already be falling. Students often incorrectly choose less than zero because total product declines immediately after the maximum, but at the maximum itself marginal product is zero.

text: Garcia is currently spending his entire lunch budget on 3 sodas and 4 hot dogs. At his current level of consumption, Garcia’s marginal utility for sodas is 5 utils and his marginal utility for hot dogs is 10 utils. In order to maximize his total utility, Garcia should

options.A: consume more sodas and fewer hot dogs regardless of the prices
options.B: consume more hot dogs and fewer sodas regardless of the prices
options.C: maintain his current level of consumption of sodas and hot dogs regardless of the prices
options.D: maintain his current level of consumption if the price of a soda is $1 and the price of a hot dog is $2
options.E: maintain his current level of consumption if the price of a soda is $2 and the price of a hot dog is $1

explanation: A consumer maximizes utility when the marginal utility per dollar spent is equal for all goods. With marginal utilities of 5 for soda and 10 for hot dogs, Garcia’s current bundle is optimal only if a hot dog costs twice as much as a soda, which matches the $1 and $2 prices in choice D. Choice E is tempting because hot dogs deliver higher marginal utility, but if sodas cost $2 and hot dogs only $1, hot dogs provide far more utility per dollar, so Garcia should buy more hot dogs rather than maintain his current consumption.

text: As output of a firm increases, the difference between the firm’s average total cost and its average variable cost gets smaller because the firm’s

options.A: total cost is increasing
options.B: marginal cost is increasing
options.C: average fixed cost is decreasing
options.D: marginal product of labor is decreasing
options.E: long-run average total cost is decreasing

explanation: Average total cost equals average variable cost plus average fixed cost, so the distance between them is average fixed cost. As output grows, fixed costs are spread over more units, which steadily lowers average fixed cost and shrinks that gap. Option A might seem plausible because total cost does increase with output, but that does not explain why the specific difference between these two average costs gets smaller.

text: In a perfectly competitive market, a change in which of the following could cause a shift in the supply curve?

options.A: The incomes of consumers
options.B: The number of buyers
options.C: Technology
options.D: The price of the product
options.E: Tastes and preferences

explanation: Technology is a key determinant of supply because improvements allow firms to produce more output at every price, shifting the supply curve. Many students incorrectly choose a change in the product's price, but that only causes movement along the existing supply curve rather than shifting it. Consumer incomes, number of buyers, and tastes all affect the demand curve instead.

text: Productive efficiency occurs when a firm produces output at a level at which

options.A: average total cost equals average revenue
options.B: average total cost is at a minimum
options.C: price exceeds average total cost
options.D: price equals marginal cost
options.E: marginal revenue exceeds average revenue

explanation: Productive efficiency means producing goods at the lowest possible cost per unit, which happens when average total cost is at its minimum. At this output level, the firm cannot reduce costs further by changing its production level, so no resources are wasted. Many students mistakenly choose price equals marginal cost, but that describes allocative efficiency—the socially optimal output level—rather than the least-cost production that defines productive efficiency.

text: Which of the following is true of a monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium?

options.A: Price equals marginal cost and average total cost.
options.B: Price equals average total cost but is greater than marginal cost.
options.C: Price equals marginal cost and is greater than average total cost.
options.D: The firm makes no attempt to differentiate its products.
options.E: The firm earns positive economic profits by producing at minimum average cost.

explanation: In the long run, free entry and exit eliminate economic profits, so price equals average total cost. Because the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve and maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, price is greater than marginal cost. Students often mistakenly pick option A by confusing monopolistic competition with perfect competition, where price does equal marginal cost.

text: Assume that firms sell their output in a perfectly competitive product market and hire labor in a perfectly competitive labor market. If all other factors remain constant, an increase in the demand for the firms’ product will result in which of the following changes in the labor market?

options.A: Firms will move down along the demand curve for labor and hire more workers.
options.B: The supply curve for labor will shift to the right.
options.C: The demand curve for labor will shift to the right.
options.D: The supply curve for labor will shift to the left.
options.E: The demand curve for labor will shift to the left.

explanation: An increase in demand for the firms' product raises the market price of the good, which increases the marginal revenue product of labor. Because labor demand is derived from the marginal revenue product, the labor demand curve shifts to the right. Choice A is tempting because firms do end up hiring more workers, but that hiring results from a shift of the demand curve, not a movement down along the existing curve.

text: A profit-maximizing firm will continue to hire workers until the

options.A: marginal factor cost of labor is equal to the marginal revenue product of labor
options.B: marginal factor cost of labor is equal to the price of the good produced using labor
options.C: marginal product of labor is equal to the marginal revenue product of labor
options.D: marginal product of labor is equal to the marginal factor cost of labor

explanation: The hiring rule for profit maximization is to keep adding workers as long as each one brings in more revenue than they cost, stopping exactly where marginal revenue product equals marginal factor cost. This ensures the last worker contributes just enough revenue to cover their additional cost, adding nothing more to total profit. Be careful not to confuse marginal product, which measures extra output in physical units, with marginal revenue product or marginal factor cost, which are measured in dollars.

text: Assume that the marginal social benefit of the last unit of vaccination provided is greater than the marginal social cost. Which of the following can be used to achieve efficiency in the market for vaccination?

options.A: A per-unit subsidy for vaccinations
options.B: A lump-sum tax for vaccinations
options.C: A limit on the quantity of vaccinations
options.D: A price floor for vaccinations
options.E: A price ceiling for vaccinations

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: A per-unit subsidy encourages more vaccinations by lowering the price consumers pay or raising the price suppliers receive, which increases quantity toward the socially optimal level where MSB equals MSC. Since MSB currently exceeds MSC, the market is underproducing, so a policy that boosts output is needed. A price ceiling or quantity limit would reduce supply further, and a lump-sum tax does not affect marginal incentives, so none of those would correct the underproduction.

text: Which of the following government actions can correct the inefficiency caused by the existence of a monopoly?

options.A: Granting a per-unit subsidy on the monopolist’s output
options.B: Granting an annual lump-sum subsidy to the monopolist
options.C: Imposing a per-unit tax on the monopolist’s output
options.D: Imposing a price floor on the monopolist

explanation: A per-unit subsidy lowers the monopolist’s marginal cost, giving the firm an incentive to increase output closer to the socially efficient level where price equals marginal cost. A lump-sum subsidy might seem helpful, but because it does not affect marginal cost or marginal revenue, it leaves the monopolist’s output and price unchanged and therefore does not fix the inefficiency.

text: Given the production possibilities curve above, which of the following represents a movement from efficiency to inefficiency?

options.A: Point X to point W
options.B: Point X to point Z
options.C: Point Y to point Z
options.D: Point W to point Z
options.E: Point V to point Y

text: Based on a comparison of points X, Y, and Z, the opportunity cost of an additional consumer good is

options.A: highest at point X
options.B: highest at point Y
options.C: highest at point Z
options.D: lowest at point Y

text: The table above shows the quantity of gasoline supplied and demanded at various prices in a country. If the government sets a price floor of $2.75 on a gallon of gasoline, what is the price per gallon?
unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: A price floor is a minimum price set by the government. If the government sets a price floor of $2.75, the price per gallon cannot fall below that amount. The table shows that at $2.75, the quantity supplied (12,000) is less than the quantity demanded (16,000), creating a shortage, but the price is still $2.75 because the floor is binding. The price does not rise to the equilibrium price of $3.50 because the government is forcing the price to stay at $2.75.

text: Last year 17 million tons of beans were sold for $300 per ton. This year 17 million tons of beans were sold for $285 per ton. Which of the follow­ ing changes in demand and supply could have caused this outcome? Demand Supply

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: Increase Decrease
options.C: Decrease Increase
options.D: Decrease Decrease

explanation: When demand decreases and supply increases, the price falls because buyers want less and sellers offer more at any given price. If those two shifts are roughly equal in size, the quantity traded can stay the same while the equilibrium price drops. A common wrong choice is a decrease in both demand and supply, but that would typically push quantity down rather than leave it unchanged.

text: Which of the following will most likely happen in the market for good X if the price of good X decreases?

options.A: The supply of good X will decrease.
options.B: The demand for good X will increase.
options.C: The quantity demanded for good X will increase.
options.D: The demand will decrease and the supply will increase.
options.E: The quantity supplied for good X will increase.

explanation: A decrease in the price of good X causes a movement along the demand curve, which economists call an increase in quantity demanded, not an increase in demand itself. This follows the Law of Demand: when price falls, consumers buy more.
