options.D: the marginal product of capital increases
options.E: the product’s demand decreases

explanation: Because labor and capital are substitutes, a higher price for capital makes labor relatively cheaper, leading the firm to substitute labor for capital. You might think a higher marginal product of capital would increase labor demand, but that actually makes capital more attractive to employ, not labor.

text: Assume that the firms in an industry pollute a river. If there is no government intervention, the firms will

options.A: produce more output than is socially efficient
options.B: pay production costs that are higher than actual social costs
options.C: charge a lower price than is necessary to maximize profit
options.D: charge a higher price to pay for the pollution
options.E: increase production to achieve allocative efficiency

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Firms ignore the external cost of pollution when there is no government intervention, so they base production decisions only on their private costs, which are lower than the true social costs. This causes them to produce too much output relative to the socially efficient level where social costs equal social benefits. You might be tempted by choice B, but firms actually pay private costs that are lower than total social costs, not higher.

text: The following table shows Kent’s annual income over two years and the income taxes paid in each year. Annual Income Income Taxes Year 1 $100,000 $20,000 Year 2 $120,000 $30,000 With no changes in the marginal tax-rate schedule, which of the following is true about the tax rates?

options.A: The marginal tax rate was equal to the average tax rate for both incomes.
options.B: The marginal tax rate on the last $20,000 earned was greater than the marginal tax rate at $100,000 income, but the average tax rate decreased with the increase in income.
options.C: The average tax rate when Kent earned $120,000 was less than the marginal tax rate on the last $20,000 he earned.
options.D: The amount paid in income tax increased as income increased, so the tax is proportional.
options.E: The amount paid in income tax increased as income increased, so the tax is regressive.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Kent’s average tax rate at $120,000 is $30,000 divided by $120,000, or 25 percent, while the marginal tax rate on the last $20,000 of earnings is the extra $10,000 in tax divided by $20,000, or 50 percent. Since 25 percent is less than 50 percent, the average tax rate is lower than the marginal rate on that final portion of income, so option C is correct. Option D might seem appealing because total tax paid rose with income, but a proportional tax requires a constant average tax rate, which did not occur here.

text: Dana and Robin produce smoothies and pizza. In one hour Dana can make 20 smoothies or 10 pizzas. In one hour Robin can make 18 smoothies or 6 pizzas. Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Robin has an absolute advantage in making smoothies and a comparative advantage in making pizzas.
options.B: Robin has both an absolute advantage and a comparative advantage in making pizzas.
options.C: Dana has a comparative advantage in making both smoothies and pizzas.
options.D: Dana has a comparative advantage in making pizzas, and Robin has a comparative advantage in making smoothies.

explanation: Dana's opportunity cost of one pizza is two smoothies, while Robin's is three smoothies, so Dana has the comparative advantage in pizza. Robin's opportunity cost of one smoothie is one-third of a pizza, while Dana's is one-half, so Robin has the comparative advantage in smoothies. Students often incorrectly pick A or B by confusing absolute advantage—Dana can actually make more of both goods—with comparative advantage, which depends on opportunity cost.

text: In which of the following cases would a firm’s total revenue increase?

options.A: Price increases and demand is elastic.
options.B: Price decreases and supply is inelastic.
options.C: Price decreases and demand is elastic.
options.D: Price decreases and supply is elastic.
options.E: Price decreases and demand is inelastic.

explanation: When demand is elastic, consumers are highly responsive to price, so a price decrease causes quantity demanded to rise by a larger percentage than the price fell, which increases total revenue. A common error is choosing option E, where demand is inelastic; in that case, the quantity sold increases too little to offset the lower price, so total revenue actually decreases. Options B and D are incorrect because supply elasticity does not determine how a firm’s total revenue changes when price changes.

text: In the diagram above, if there is a price ceiling set at P 1, consumer surplus will be represented by the area

options.A: A B C
options.B: P 2 B P zero
options.C: P 3 B P 2
options.D: P 3 A C P 1
options.E: P 3 B C P 1

text: Consumer surplus in a market for a good exists because

options.A: binding price floors encourage producers to increase the supply of the good
options.B: some consumers would be willing to pay more than the equilibrium price of the good
options.C: when the price of the good decreases, most consumers increase their demand for the good
options.D: producers do not have market power to set their own price
options.E: some producers charge different prices for the good in different markets

explanation: Consumer surplus exists because the demand curve shows that many buyers value a good more than the market price they actually pay, and the difference between that higher willingness to pay and the lower equilibrium price is their net benefit. This gap is what creates the triangular area of surplus below the demand curve and above the price. Choice C may tempt students because it talks about consumers and price changes, but it confuses the law of demand with the concept of willingness to pay that generates surplus.

text: Assume Pat spends all of her allowance to purchase 4 apples and 4 candy bars. Pat’s marginal utility of the fourth apple is 20 utils, and her marginal utility of the fourth candy bar is 40 utils. If an apple costs $1.00 and a candy bar $0.50, to maximize utility Pat should

options.A: purchase more apples and more candy bars
options.B: maintain the current purchase of 4 apples and 4 candy bars
options.C: purchase more apples and fewer candy bars
options.D: purchase fewer apples and more candy bars
options.E: purchase fewer apples and fewer candy bars

explanation: Pat gets 80 utils per dollar from the last candy bar but only 20 utils per dollar from the last apple, so she should shift spending toward candy bars and away from apples until the marginal utility per dollar is equal for both. Buying fewer apples and more candy bars raises the marginal utility of apples and lowers that of candy bars, moving her toward the optimal mix. Choice B is tempting if you only compare the raw marginal utilities, but utility maximization depends on marginal utility per dollar, not just total marginal utility.

text: A firm is producing 100 units of output at a total cost of $400. The firm’s average variable cost is $3 per unit. What is the firm’s total fixed cost?
explanation: Total fixed cost equals total cost minus total variable cost. Since average variable cost is $3 and output is 100 units, total variable cost is $300. Subtracting that from the $400 total cost leaves $100 in fixed cost. A common mistake is choosing $300, which is the firm's total variable cost rather than its fixed cost.

text: A profit-maximizing firm will shut down in the short run any time the firm’s total revenue is less than its

options.A: total cost
options.B: fixed cost
options.C: total variable cost
options.D: explicit cost
options.E: implicit cost Quantity of Output (units) Total Variable Cost $0 $40 $50 $65 $90

explanation: A firm shuts down in the short run only when total revenue is less than total variable cost because fixed costs are sunk and must be paid whether the firm produces or not. If revenue covers variable costs, the firm reduces its losses by operating since it can put the remainder toward fixed costs. Total cost is a tempting wrong answer because firms do exit in the long run when revenue is less than total cost, but in the short run the shutdown decision depends only on variable costs.

text: Assume that the fixed cost is $50. Based on the cost and output data in the table above, what is the marginal cost when the firm increases its output from three to four units and the average total cost of producing 4 units? Marginal Cost Average Total Cost

options.E: $10 $25 Nature View Bids High Bids Low Evergreen Bids High $600, $300 $520, $400 Bids Low $720, $100 $500, $200

explanation: To find the marginal cost of producing the fourth unit, subtract the total variable cost at 3 units ($65) from the total variable cost at 4 units ($90), which equals $25. The average total cost for 4 units is calculated by adding the fixed cost ($50) to the total variable cost ($90) to get a total cost of $140, then dividing by the 4 units of output, which equals $35. Therefore, the marginal cost is $25 and the average total cost is $35.

text: Evergreen and Nature View are bidding for a landscaping contract. The payoff matrix above shows what each firm’s total weekly profits from all its operations will be for each combination of bids. The first entry in each cell shows Evergreen’s profit, and the second entry in each cell shows Nature View’s profit. A Nash equilibrium results under which of the following conditions?

options.A: When Evergreen bids low, no matter what Nature View’s bid is
options.B: When both firms bid high and when both firms bid low
options.C: When Evergreen bids high and Nature View bids low
options.D: When both firms bid low
options.E: When both firms bid high

text: Suppose that the demand for soft drinks is price elastic and the supply is price inelastic. If the government imposes a sales tax on soft drinks, which of the following will occur in the short run?

options.A: The tax burden will fall equally on both consumers and producers.
options.B: The tax burden will fall more on producers.
options.C: The tax burden will fall more on consumers.
options.D: The percentage increase in the price of soft drinks will be greater than the percentage increase in the quantity demanded.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The tax burden falls mainly on producers because they have the more inelastic supply, meaning they cannot easily adjust output when costs rise. Consumers with elastic demand can simply buy fewer soft drinks if prices go up, so they avoid most of the tax. Many students incorrectly choose the consumer because a sales tax is paid at the store, but legal incidence does not determine who actually bears the economic burden.

text: If both supply and demand for wheat increase, the equilibrium price and quantity of wheat will most likely change in which of the following ways? Price Quantity

options.A: Decrease Decrease
options.B: Decrease Increase
options.C: Indeterminate Increase
options.D: Increase Decrease
options.E: Increase Indeterminate

explanation: When both supply and demand increase, both shifts push equilibrium quantity higher, so quantity definitely rises. However, the demand shift raises price while the supply shift lowers it, so the net effect on price depends on which shift is larger, making price indeterminate. A common mistake is choosing (E), which incorrectly swaps the outcomes—price is the uncertain one, not quantity, since both shifts unambiguously increase output.

text: The last worker currently employed by a firm has a marginal product of 3 units per hour and is paid $20 per hour. Assuming that both the labor market and product market are perfectly competitive and that the product’s price is $5 per unit, the firm should do which of the following?

options.A: Decrease wages
options.B: Increase wages
options.C: Employ more workers
options.D: Employ fewer workers
options.E: Increase the product’s price

explanation: The firm should employ fewer workers because the last worker's marginal revenue product is only $15 per hour (3 units × $5), which is less than the $20 wage. When a worker's MRP is below the wage, the firm loses money on that hire and has moved past the profit-maximizing level of employment. It is tempting to choose employing more workers because the worker still produces something, but hiring beyond the point where MRP equals the wage reduces the firm's profit.

text: Hope Hospital is a monopsonistic employer of nurses. The marginal revenue product of nursing services, the marginal factor (resource) cost of nursing services, and the market supply curve of nursing services are depicted in the figure above byM R P, M F C, and S, respectively. What wagequantity combination does Hope Hospital choose in order to maximize its profits?

options.A: W 1 and Q 1
options.B: W 1 and Q 3
options.C: W 2 and Q 2
options.D: W 2 and Q 4
options.E: W 3 and Q 3 Number of Workers Total Product 15 20 24 27 29

explanation: A monopsonistic employer maximizes profit by hiring the quantity of labor where the marginal revenue product (MRP) equals the marginal factor cost (MFC). In the graph, this occurs at quantity Q2. The wage rate is determined by the supply curve (S) at that quantity, which is W2. Therefore, the profit-maximizing combination is W2 and Q2. Choice E is incorrect because it represents the competitive equilibrium, where MRP equals the supply curve, not MFC.

text: The table above shows the short-run output for a perfectly competitive firm. If the price of the product is $10, what is the marginal revenue product of the third worker hired?
explanation: The marginal revenue product (MRP) of a worker is calculated by multiplying the marginal product (MP) of that worker by the price of the product. From the table, the total product increases from 20 to 24 when the third worker is hired, so the marginal product of the third worker is 4 units. With a product price of $10, the MRP is 4 units × $10 = $40. Option (A) is the marginal product, not the MRP, and option (D) incorrectly multiplies the total product by the price.

text: Which of the following is true based on the graph above?

options.A: Quantity of education in the private market is more than the socially optimal quantity.
options.B: Consumers of education could be subsidized in order to achieve the socially optimal quantity.
options.C: Producers of education could be taxed in order to achieve the socially optimal quantity.
options.D: Consumers of education could be taxed in order to achieve the socially optimal quantity.
options.E: Consumption of education has a negative externality.

text: An outward shift of a production possibilities curve can be caused by

options.A: planting a more profitable farm crop
options.B: improving technology
options.C: using idle resources
options.D: changing consumer preferences
options.E: increasing the minimum wage

explanation: Improving technology allows an economy to produce more goods and services with the same amount of resources, which shifts the entire production possibilities curve outward. A common tempting wrong answer is using idle resources, but that simply moves production from a point inside the curve to a point on the curve rather than expanding the economy's maximum potential output.

text: At a price of $10, the quantity demanded of pizzas is 100 and the quantity supplied is 150. Which of the following statements must be true?

options.A: There is a shortage of pizza at a price of $10.
options.B: The equilibrium price of pizza is below $10.
options.C: The quantity of pizzas sold will be 150.
options.D: At equilibrium, fewer than 100 pizzas will be sold.
options.E: The pizza market is in equilibrium. Total Utility QUANTITY OF CHOCOLATE (ounces)

explanation: A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, which tells us the current price is above equilibrium. Consequently, the equilibrium price must be lower than $10 to clear the market. It is tempting to choose shortage, but a shortage exists only when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied.

text: The diagram above shows Sally’s utility function for chocolate. Her utility function illustrates the principle of

options.A: trade-offs when making choices
options.B: diminishing marginal utility
options.C: income and substitution effects
options.D: increasing opportunity cost
options.E: constrained utility maximization

text: At a perfectly competitive firm’s current output level, average total cost is $15, average variable cost is $10, and marginal cost is $8 and increasing. If the product price is $15, what should this firm do to maximize profits?

options.A: Increase the quantity of output produced.
options.B: Increase the product price.
options.C: Decrease the product price to increase sales.
options.D: Shut down immediately.
options.E: Continue to produce at its current output level.

explanation: A perfectly competitive firm maximizes profit by producing where price equals marginal cost. Because the $15 price exceeds the $8 marginal cost, each additional unit adds more to total revenue than to total cost, so the firm should increase output until marginal cost rises to equal price. Continuing at the current output is tempting because price equals average total cost, but that only means zero economic profit at this moment, not that profit is maximized.

text: The government must provide public goods such as national defense because

options.A: the production of public goods requires economies of scale that the private sector cannot achieve
options.B: it is generally impossible to exclude individuals who value public goods but do not pay for them
options.C: public goods cannot be produced in private competitive markets, since they have highly inelastic demand
options.D: private producers charge a price that is substantially greater than marginal cost
options.E: no single individual should have to pay for public goods, since they benefit society as a whole

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Public goods are non-excludable, which means it is nearly impossible to prevent people from benefiting even if they do not pay. This free-rider problem makes private provision unprofitable, so the government must step in. Option E might seem appealing because society as a whole benefits, but the core economic reason is market failure due to non-excludability, not fairness.

text: Which of the following will increase the demand for pizza, a normal good?

options.A: An increase in the cost of producing pizza
options.B: A decrease in the price of pizza
options.C: An increase in the price of a complementary product
options.D: An increase in consumers’ income

explanation: For a normal good like pizza, demand rises when consumers have more income to spend. An increase in consumers' income shifts the demand curve to the right. Many students incorrectly choose a decrease in the price of pizza, but that only increases the quantity demanded along the existing curve rather than increasing overall demand itself.

text: Game theory is used to explain

options.A: why firms price discriminate
options.B: how monopolies evolve into oligopolies
options.C: strategic behavior of firms in oligopoly
options.D: profit maximization in monopoly
options.E: price leadership of monopolistic competition

explanation: Game theory studies decision-making when each participant's outcome depends on the choices of others, which captures the mutual interdependence that defines oligopoly. It is specifically used to model strategic behavior such as pricing and output decisions where firms must anticipate how rivals will react. A tempting wrong choice might be price leadership in monopolistic competition, but that market structure has too many firms for strategic interdependence, whereas game theory applies to the small number of rivals in an oligopoly.

text: If a profit-maximizing firm in a perfectly competitive market chooses to produce in the short run, then marginal cost is always

options.A: greater than or equal to total cost
options.B: greater than or equal to average total cost
options.C: greater than or equal to average variable cost
options.D: greater than or equal to average fixed cost
options.E: less than average total cost

explanation: In the short run, a perfectly competitive firm only produces if the market price is at or above the minimum of its average variable cost curve, and because it sets price equal to marginal cost to maximize profit, marginal cost must be greater than or equal to average variable cost. You might be tempted to think marginal cost must exceed average total cost, but that is not required; a firm will keep producing while taking a loss as long as price covers average variable cost, meaning marginal cost can sit well below average total cost.

text: The table above shows the total benefit Tony gets from eating different quantities of apples. If apples cost $3 each, how many should he buy to maximize his consumer surplus?
explanation: To maximize consumer surplus, Tony should buy the quantity where the marginal benefit (the additional benefit from one more apple) is at least as great as the price. The marginal benefit of the first apple is $10, the second is $8 ($18 - $10), the third is $6 ($24 - $18), the fourth is $4 ($28 - $24), and the fifth is $2 ($30 - $28). Since the price is $3, he should buy up to the fourth apple, where the marginal benefit ($4) is greater than the price. However, the marginal benefit of the fifth apple is only $2, which is less than the price, so he should not buy it. The consumer surplus is maximized at 4 apples, but the official answer is C (3). This suggests a possible error in the provided answer key, as the correct quantity should be 4. Given the data, the correct answer should be D (4), not C (3).

text: Given the demand curve above, if price decreases from $8 to $4 per unit, total consumer surplus will

options.A: increase by $4
options.B: increase by $8
options.C: increase by $12
options.D: increase by $18
options.E: remain constant at $24

text: Which of the following describes how a market will respond when the scarcity of a good increases?

options.A: Consumers will increase their demand for the good.
options.B: Consumers will decrease their demand for the good.
options.C: The price of the good will increase.
options.D: The price of the good will decrease.
options.E: Producers will increase the supply of the good.

explanation: When a good becomes scarcer, the available quantity falls relative to consumer demand, which causes buyers to bid up the market price. A tempting wrong answer is A, but scarcity alone does not increase demand, because demand depends on consumer preferences and income rather than on how limited the good's supply is.

text: Suppose that the demand for vegetables is price elastic. If the price of vegetables increases by 5 percent, the quantity of vegetables demanded would

options.A: increase by 5 percent
options.B: increase by more than 5 percent
options.C: increase by less than 5 percent
options.D: decrease by more than 5 percent
options.E: decrease by less than 5 percent

explanation: When demand is price elastic, the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price, and the law of demand means quantity moves in the opposite direction of price. Therefore, a 5 percent price increase leads to a decrease in quantity demanded of more than 5 percent. Choice E might tempt students who recall that quantity falls but confuse elastic demand with inelastic demand, which would produce a decrease of less than 5 percent.

text: The table below lists the monthly individual demand schedules for text messages for the only three buyers in the market: Allison, Bill, and Chang. | Price per Text Message | Text Messages Demanded by | |------------------------|---------------------------| | | Allison | Bill | Chang | | 4¢ | 500 | 400 | 360 | | 8¢ | 350 | 300 | 280 | | 12¢ | 200 | 200 | 200 | | 16¢ | 50 | 100 | 120 | | 20¢ | 0 | 0 | 40 | Which of the following combinations of price and quantity lies on the market demand curve? | Price | Quantity | |-------|----------| |
explanation: The market demand curve shows the total quantity demanded by all consumers at each price. At a price of 16¢, the total quantity demanded is the sum of the individual quantities: 50 (Allison) + 100 (Bill) + 120 (Chang) = 270. This matches option (D). Option (A) is incorrect because it sums the quantities at 4¢ (500 + 400 + 360 = 1,260), not 1,000. Option (C) is the quantity demanded by one person at 12¢, not the market total.

text: Which of the following best explains why a firm's short-run marginal cost curve shifts down when it purchases new, more efficient equipment and experiences an increase in its total cost?

options.A: The situation represents an exception to the law of diminishing returns.
options.B: The average total cost curve shifts upward as a result of the equipment purchase, and there is a movement up along the marginal cost curve.
options.C: The equipment purchase is a fixed cost, and the new equipment will cause a reduction in the cost of producing each additional unit.
options.D: The average variable cost curve shifts upward as a result of the equipment purchase, and the marginal cost curve shifts downward.
options.E: The marginal cost curve shifts downward because of the law of diminishing returns. Questions 15-16 are based on the chart below for a firm that is perfectly competitive in both the labor and product markets, showing how much daily output a firm can produce using different numbers of workers. | Number of Workers | Output | |-------------------|--------| | 1 | 3 | | 2 | 9 | | 3 | 16 | | 4 | 21 | | 5 | 23 | | 6 | 24 |

explanation: The purchase of new equipment is a fixed cost, which raises total cost while the improved efficiency lowers the cost of producing each additional unit, shifting the marginal cost curve downward. Choice E may tempt students because diminishing returns is closely tied to marginal cost, but it actually explains why the curve slopes upward rather than why better technology would shift the entire curve down.

text: If output sells for $20 per unit, what is the marginal revenue product of the fifth worker?
If output sells for $20 per unit and the daily wage is $100 per worker, how many workers should the firm hire to maximize profit?
Given the information above, the average variable cost of 25 units of output is

A typical firm in a perfectly competitive constant-cost industry is operating with an economic loss in the short run. When the industry returns to long-run equilibrium, what will happen to the number of firms in the industry, the market price, and the typical firm’s quantity? Number of Firms Market Price Firm’s Quantity

options.A: Decrease Increase Increase
options.B: Decrease Decrease Increase
options.C: Decrease Increase Decrease
options.D: Increase Increase Decrease
options.E: Increase Decrease Decrease Questions 19-20 refer to the table below. The two firms in an industry are deciding whether to advertise. The profit to each firm depends on the other firm’s decision. The first entries in the matrix below indicate the profit earned, in millions of dollars, by Firm A; and the second entries indicate the profits earned, in millions of dollars, by Firm B. Firm B Advertise Do Not Advertise Firm A Advertise $7, $1 $5, $4 Do Not Advertise $3, $2 $2, $0

explanation: Firms that are losing money will leave the industry, so the number of firms falls and market supply shifts left, causing the market price to rise. The typical remaining firm faces a higher price and moves up its marginal cost curve, so it increases its output. Choice B might look tempting if you think fewer firms mean lower prices, but less supply actually pushes the price up.

text: Based on the payoff matrix, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Firm A always gets a smaller share of the industry profits.
options.B: Firm A’s dominant strategy is to advertise.
options.C: Firm B’s dominant strategy is not to advertise.
options.D: The dominant strategy for both firms is not to advertise.
options.E: Neither firm has a dominant strategy.

text: The combination where Firm A advertises and Firm B does not advertise is Nash equilibrium because

options.A: it is best for each firm given what the other firm has chosen
options.B: the total industry profits are maximized
options.C: Firm A has an incentive to change its strategy and chooses not to advertise
options.D: it is the best outcome for Firm B regardless of what firm A does

explanation: A Nash equilibrium means each firm is doing the best it can given the other firm’s choice, so Firm A advertises because that is its best response to Firm B not advertising, and Firm B does not advertise because that is its best response to Firm A advertising, which is exactly what option A states. A common mistake is selecting the answer about maximizing total industry profits, but a Nash equilibrium only requires that neither firm wants to change its own strategy unilaterally, not that the combined payoff is highest.

options.A: 30 pencils
options.B: 10 pencils
options.C: 3 pencils
options.D: 1/3 of a pencil
options.E: 1/10 of a pencil PRICE $10 0 1 2 3 4 5 QUANTITY Demand Curve Y Demand Curve X

options.A: Perfectly elastic Perfectly inelastic
options.B: Perfectly inelastic Perfectly elastic
options.C: Perfectly inelastic Relatively elastic
options.D: Relatively inelastic Perfectly elastic

text: An art student spends all of her income on pencils and drawing pads. The student currently buys 30 pencils at $1 each and 10 pads at $5 each. If the marginal utility of the 30th pencil is 100 utils and the marginal utility of the 10th pad is 400 utils, to maximize utility the student should change her purchases of pencils and pads in which of the following ways? Pencils Pads

options.A: Not change Buy more
options.B: Buy more Buy more
options.C: Buy more Buy less
options.D: Buy less Buy more
options.E: Buy less Buy less

explanation: To maximize utility, a consumer must equalize marginal utility per dollar across goods. The pencil’s marginal utility per dollar is 100 utils divided by $1, or 100, while the pad’s is 400 utils divided by $5, or 80. Because pencils provide more additional satisfaction per dollar, the student should buy more pencils and fewer pads. Choice D is tempting if you compare the raw marginal utilities of 100 and 400 and forget to account for the price difference, but that comparison is incorrect.

text: Assume that the current market equilibrium price for milk is $2.80 per gallon and that 5 million gallons are sold per day. If the government sets a price ceiling of $2.00 per gallon, which of the following is true?

options.A: The demand for milk will increase.
options.B: The supply of milk will decrease.
options.C: There will be an excess supply of milk in the market.
options.D: More than 5 million gallons of milk will be sold.
options.E: Less than 5 million gallons of milk will be sold.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Because the $2.00 ceiling is below the $2.80 equilibrium price, it is binding: producers reduce the quantity they offer while consumers want to buy more, so the market is limited by the smaller amount suppliers are willing to sell. This means fewer than 5 million gallons will actually be traded. It is easy to confuse a price ceiling with a price floor and choose excess supply, but a below-equilibrium ceiling creates a shortage, not a surplus.

text: Which of the following is most likely to cause the demand curve for nurses to shift to the right?

options.A: An increase in the number of nurses graduating from nursing schools
options.B: An increase in nursing schools' tuition
options.C: An increase in the number of hospitals that employ nurses
options.D: A decrease in the marginal productivity of nurses
options.E: An improvement in the health of older people

explanation: An increase in the number of hospitals means there are more employers seeking to hire nurses, which increases the demand for nurses at every wage and shifts the demand curve to the right. It is important to remember that the demand for labor comes from employers, not the workers themselves. A common wrong choice is A, because more nursing graduates increases the supply of nurses, not the demand for them.

text: In a given year, Jennifer earns $50,000 and spends $40,000. During the same period, Steve earns $30,000 and spends $27,000. If Jennifer and Steve both must pay a 10 percent sales tax on goods purchased, the sales tax is

options.A: a higher percentage of income for Jennifer than for Steve
options.B: a higher percentage of spending for Steve than for Jennifer
options.C: progressive with respect to income
options.D: regressive with respect to income
options.E: proportional with respect to income

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Steve pays $2,700 in sales tax, which equals 9 percent of his $30,000 income, while Jennifer pays $4,000, which equals only 8 percent of her $50,000 income. Because the tax claims a larger share of income from the lower earner, it is regressive with respect to income. Many students incorrectly choose proportional or progressive because the stated sales tax rate is a flat 10 percent, but what matters for tax incidence is the percentage of total income paid in taxes.

text: A monopolistically competitive firm is currently producing the profit-maximizing level of output. If the price of a variable input increases, which of the following will occur?

options.A: The firm will increase its output to increase its revenue.
options.B: The firm will increase the price of its output by the same amount.
options.C: The firm's average total cost and marginal cost curves will shift upward.
options.D: The firm's average fixed cost will decrease as it decreases production.
options.E: The firm's fixed cost will increase, but its output level will be unaffected.

explanation: An increase in a variable input's price raises both marginal and average total costs, so those cost curves shift upward. Fixed costs are unaffected because they do not rely on variable inputs. Choice E might tempt students who confuse all costs with fixed costs, but fixed costs stay the same by definition. Choice A is also incorrect because the firm will reduce, not increase, its output after the marginal cost curve shifts up.

text: The table below shows the long-run total cost function of a firm. Quantity of Output Total Cost ($) 0 0 1 10 2 20 3 30 4 40 5 50 The firm's cost function exhibits

options.A: diseconomies of scale
options.B: constant returns to scale
options.C: economies of scale
options.D: decreasing marginal cost

explanation: The table shows that total cost increases by $10 for each additional unit of output, meaning the average total cost remains constant at $10 per unit. This constant average cost indicates constant returns to scale. Option D is incorrect because marginal cost is constant, not decreasing, and the question asks about long-run returns to scale, not short-run cost behavior.

text: In the short run, the firm will

options.A: shut down if the price falls below P₃
options.B: continue to produce as long as the price is greater than P₁
options.C: continue to produce as long as the price is greater than P₂
options.D: earn economic profits as long as the price is greater than P₂
options.E: cover its fixed cost as long as the price is less than P₃

explanation: In the short run, a firm continues to produce as long as price covers average variable cost, since operating losses are smaller than the fixed costs that would be lost by shutting down. Option C correctly states this shutdown rule. Option B is tempting but sets the cutoff too high, so it would wrongly advise the firm to close when price is still sufficient to cover variable costs. Option D is also incorrect because merely covering variable costs does not create economic profit, which requires price to exceed average total cost.

text: The firm’s short-run supply curve is which of the following?

options.A: The AVC curve above P₁
options.B: The AVC curve above P₂
options.C: The ATC curve above P₃
options.D: The MC curve above P₂
options.E: The MC curve above P₃ Labor Hours Required to Produce One Pair of Shoes One Loaf of Bread Mr. X 5 hours 1 hour Ms. Y 2 hours 0.5 hour

explanation: A firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its marginal cost curve that lies above the minimum average variable cost, which is the shutdown point. Because the shutdown price is P₂, the supply curve is the MC curve above P₂. Options mentioning AVC or ATC are incorrect because supply is determined by marginal cost, not average cost, and option E is wrong because it uses a price threshold other than the true shutdown point.

text: According to the data above, if Mr. X and Ms. Y have the opportunity to trade, which of the following will be mutually beneficial?

options.A: Ms. Y sells shoes to and buys bread from Mr. X.
options.B: Ms. Y sells bread to and buys shoes from Mr. X.
options.C: Ms. Y sells both bread and shoes to Mr. X.
options.D: Ms. Y buys both bread and shoes from Mr. X.
options.E: Ms. Y and Mr. X do not trade with each other.

text: If the government eliminates an effective minimum wage in a competitive labor market, which of the following is true?

options.A: Minimum wage workers will experience no change in hourly pay.
options.B: Minimum wage workers will experience a decrease in hourly pay.
options.C: The number of people employed will decrease because people do not want to work for low wages.
options.D: There will be an excess demand for workers.
options.E: There will be an increase in the supply of workers.

explanation: Eliminating an effective minimum wage removes a price floor, allowing the wage to drop to the lower market equilibrium. Workers who had been earning the minimum wage will therefore see their hourly pay decrease. A tempting wrong choice is that employment will fall because people do not want to work for less, but the lower wage actually raises the quantity of labor demanded, so employment increases rather than decreases.

text: Carmen consumes both entertainment and medical care. For Carmen, entertainment is a normal good, and the income elasticity of her demand for medical care is zero. If Carmen’s income increases, which of the following will be the immediate impact on her consumption? Entertainment Medical Care

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: Increase No change
options.C: No change Increase
options.D: Increase Decrease

explanation: Since entertainment is a normal good, Carmen will buy more of it when her income rises. Because the income elasticity of demand for medical care is zero, her quantity demanded for medical care does not respond to income changes at all, so it stays the same. A common mistake is choosing option A by assuming medical care is also a normal good, but zero income elasticity specifically means no change in consumption when income changes.

text: Assume that a perfectly competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium. If industry demand for the product increases, how will this firm’s price, output, and profit change in the short run? Price Output Profit

options.A: Increase Increase Increase
options.B: Increase Decrease Decrease
options.C: Increase Increase Decrease
options.D: No change Decrease Decrease
options.E: Decrease Increase Increase

explanation: An increase in market demand raises the market price that each perfectly competitive firm must accept, shifting the firm's horizontal demand curve upward. The firm increases output until the new higher price equals its marginal cost, and because price rises above average total cost in the short run, economic profit increases. Students often mistakenly think the firm's price stays the same because individual firms are price takers, forgetting that the market price itself changes when industry demand shifts.

text: One difference between oligopolies and monopolistically competitive markets is that

options.A: there is no deadweight loss in monopolistically competitive markets, but there is in oligopolies
options.B: the products sold in monopolistically competitive markets are identical
options.C: oligopolies have fewer barriers to entry
options.D: firms maximize profits in monopolistically competitive markets but not in oligopolies
options.E: there are fewer firms in oligopolistic markets than in monopolistically competitive ones Questions 36-37 refer to the following diagram of a natural monopolist.

explanation: Oligopolies consist of only a few dominant firms, while monopolistically competitive markets contain many small firms, so the number of firms is the key distinction. This difference is central to how economists classify these markets. A tempting wrong choice is A, because students often assume monopolistically competitive markets are as efficient as perfect competition; however, firms in both structures set price above marginal cost, which means both can create deadweight loss.

text: The firm shown in the diagram above qualifies as a natural monopoly because

options.A: the demand curve is downward sloping
options.B: the demand curve lies above the marginal revenue curve
options.C: the average total cost is decreasing in the relevant range of market demand
options.D: the firm can maximize profit with any output level it chooses
options.E: marginal revenue is positive at the profit-maximizing output level

text: If government regulated the natural monopoly to produce the output resulting in zero economic profit, then the output would be

options.A: Q1
options.B: Q2
options.C: Q3
options.D: Q4
options.E: Q5

explanation: Zero economic profit requires regulators to set price equal to average total cost, which gives the monopoly a normal profit but no economic profit. This fair-return output is greater than the unregulated quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. At that unregulated output, the firm earns positive economic profit because its price exceeds average total cost.

text: Which of the following characteristics is prevalent in oligopolies?

options.A: Allocative efficiency
options.B: Low barriers of entry
options.C: Consideration of rivals' reactions
options.D: No deadweight loss
options.E: Zero economic profit

explanation: Oligopolies are defined by interdependence among the few large firms, so each firm must constantly consider how its rivals will react to its pricing and output choices. This strategic behavior explains why economists use game theory to model oligopolies. Students often mistakenly choose allocative efficiency, but oligopolies typically price above marginal cost and generate deadweight loss rather than achieving the efficient outcome found in perfect competition.

text: A firm uses capital and labor in its production process. The marginal product for the last unit of labor is 5, the marginal product for the last unit of capital is 10, and the wage is $10. At what cost of hiring each unit of capital would the firm be minimizing the cost of the current output?
explanation: To minimize cost, a firm hires inputs so that the marginal product per dollar is equal across them. Here, labor yields 5 units per $10, or 0.5 units per dollar, so capital must also yield 0.5 units per dollar; with a marginal product of 10, the rental rate must be $20. A student might pick $10 by wrongly assuming capital should cost the same as labor, but cost minimization depends on productivity per dollar, not equal input prices.

text: Which of the following must be true if a profit-maximizing monopolistically competitive firm continues to operate in the short run while incurring a loss?

options.A: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost and price is greater than average total cost.
options.B: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost and price is greater than average variable cost.
options.C: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost and price is less than average variable cost.
options.D: Price equals both marginal cost and marginal revenue.
options.E: Price is less than marginal revenue, but greater than average variable cost.

explanation: A profit-maximizing firm of any market structure produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. When a firm operates despite a loss, its price must still exceed average variable cost; otherwise, shutting down would minimize losses. Option A is incorrect because a price greater than average total cost indicates economic profit, not a loss.

text: Marginal analysis suggests that an individual will consume one additional unit of a good if the

options.A: sunk cost can be recovered
options.B: total benefit is less than the total cost
options.C: total benefit is greater than the total cost
options.D: additional benefit is less than the additional cost
options.E: additional benefit is greater than the additional cost

explanation: Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit and extra cost of consuming exactly one more unit, so a person will consume it only when the additional benefit is greater than the additional cost. Option C is tempting because total benefit exceeding total cost can make an activity profitable overall, but that total comparison does not reveal whether the next single unit is worth consuming.

text: If a perfectly competitive market with no government intervention is allocatively efficient, which of the following must be true?

options.A: Consumer surplus plus producer surplus is at its maximum.
options.B: Consumer surplus is larger than producer surplus.
options.C: Producer surplus is larger than consumer surplus.
options.D: All surplus is producer surplus.
options.E: All surplus is consumer surplus. Questions 43-44 are based on the output and cost data in the table below. | Quantity of Output Produced (units) | Total Variable Cost ($) | Total Cost ($) | |-------------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | 1 | 100 | 200 | | 2 | 190 | 290 | | 3 | 270 | 370 | | 4 | 340 | 440 | | 5 | 420 | 520 | | 6 | 510 | 610 | | 7 | 610 | 710 |

explanation: Allocative efficiency occurs when a market produces the quantity where the marginal benefit to consumers equals the marginal cost to producers, which is exactly what happens in a perfectly competitive equilibrium. At this point, the sum of consumer and producer surplus—total surplus—is maximized, making option A correct. Options B through E are wrong because allocative efficiency says nothing about how the surplus is divided between buyers and sellers; that depends on the shapes of the supply and demand curves.

options.A: increasing
options.B: decreasing
options.E: impossible to determine

options.A: 7th
options.B: 6th
options.C: 5th
options.D: 4th
options.E: 3rd

text: Max employs both labor and capital to produce toy trains. Currently the last unit of labor employed has a marginal product of 15 units. The last unit of capital employed has a marginal product of 40 units. The price of labor is $3 per unit, and the price of capital is $10 per unit. Which of the following employment decisions should Max follow to use the least-cost combination of labor and capital to produce the current quantity of toy trains? Employment of Labor Employment of Capital

options.A: Increase No change
options.B: Decrease Increase
options.C: Decrease Decrease
options.D: Increase Increase
options.E: Increase Decrease

explanation: To produce a given quantity at the lowest cost, a firm must allocate spending so that the marginal product per dollar is equal for all inputs. Because the last dollar spent on capital currently adds more to output than the last dollar spent on labor, Max should substitute toward capital and away from labor by decreasing labor and increasing capital. It is tempting to increase labor because its price is lower, but that would be wrong because cost minimization depends on additional output per dollar, not on the input price alone.

text: Good X is produced in a perfectly competitive industry in long-run equilibrium. If the consumption of good X generates positive externalities, the private market will produce

options.A: less than the socially optimum amount of good X
options.B: more than the socially optimum amount of good X
options.C: the socially optimum amount of good X
options.D: good X only if the government grants a subsidy for the production of good X
options.E: good X only if the government levies a corrective tax on the production of good X Questions 47-48 refer to the following graph, which shows the cost and revenue curves for a profit-maximizing monopolistically competitive firm.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: When consumption creates positive externalities, the social benefit exceeds the private benefit, so the private market ignores those extra benefits and ends up producing less than the socially optimal quantity. Option D might seem appealing because a subsidy could correct the underproduction, but the market still supplies some good X on its own; it simply falls short of the ideal amount.

text: What is the profit-maximizing price and quantity? Price Quantity

options.A: P₁ Q₁
options.B: P₂ Q₄
options.C: P₃ Q₅
options.D: P₄ Q₂
options.E: P₅ Q₁

text: Is the firm in short-run or long-run equilibrium?

options.A: Short run, because price is greater than marginal cost
options.B: Short run, because the firm is earning a positive economic profit
options.C: Long run, because price is greater than average total cost
options.D: Long run, because marginal revenue is not equal to zero

explanation: A firm earning positive economic profit cannot be in long-run equilibrium because new competitors would enter and erode those profits until they reach zero. This means the firm must be operating in the short run. Choice C might look appealing since price exceeds average total cost, but that profit signal actually indicates the market has not yet adjusted to its long-run outcome.

text: Which of the following is true of a firm in a perfectly competitive industry?

options.A: It faces a perfectly elastic demand curve.
options.B: It faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
options.C: It will increase its total revenue if it increases the selling price of its product.
options.D: Its cost could be greatly reduced if it did not have to advertise its product.
options.E: It sets the price of its product at the level at which profits are maximized or losses are minimized.

explanation: A firm in perfect competition is a price taker, so it can sell any amount of output at the prevailing market price, which means the demand curve facing the individual firm is perfectly elastic and horizontal. Choice E is tempting because it mentions profit maximization, but a competitive firm does not set the price; it accepts the market price and chooses its quantity where price equals marginal cost.

text: In the diagram above, the deadweight loss from a profit-maximizing monopolist is represented by area

options.A: FGK
options.B: FHI
options.C: IJK
options.D: GHIK
options.E: 0HIQ

text: As the population of a country ages, the demand for health care is projected to increase. As a result, the health care industry is likely to experience all of the following EXCEPT

options.A: an increase in demand for health care workers
options.B: an increase in demand for medicine
options.C: an increase in the quantity of health care workers supplied
options.D: an increase in the wages of health care workers
options.E: a decrease in the prices of medicine

explanation: Greater demand for health care services increases the demand for inputs such as medicine and medical workers, which pushes up wages in the industry. The higher wages cause a movement along the labor supply curve, so the quantity of health care workers supplied increases. Because demand for medicine is rising, its price would be expected to increase rather than decrease. Option C is tempting because it sounds like a supply shift, but it actually describes a change in quantity supplied in response to higher wages.

text: Suppose that the government imposes a per-unit tax on the producers of a good that has a perfectly inelastic demand. After the tax, the price and quantity of the good sold would change in which of the following ways? | Price | Quantity | |-------|----------| |

options.A: | Increase | Increase | |
options.B: | Increase | Decrease | |
options.C: | Increase | Not change | |
options.D: | Not change | Increase | |
options.E: | Decrease | Not change |

explanation: With perfectly inelastic demand, consumers will buy the same quantity no matter what the price is, so the quantity sold does not change when the tax is imposed. Because the demand curve is vertical, buyers bear the entire burden of the tax, which means the price they pay increases by the full amount of the tax. A common mistake is choosing that the quantity decreases, but a tax only reduces output when demand or supply is at least somewhat responsive to price changes.

text: When the marginal cost curve lies below the average total cost curve, it is true that as output increases

options.A: marginal cost is decreasing
options.B: marginal cost is increasing
options.C: average total cost is decreasing
options.D: average total cost is increasing
options.E: average variable cost is decreasing

explanation: When marginal cost is below average total cost, producing another unit adds less to total cost than the current average, which pulls the average total cost downward as output expands. Therefore, average total cost is decreasing. Choice E is tempting but wrong because marginal cost could still lie above average variable cost, meaning average variable cost might be rising even while average total cost falls.

text: Assume that the government imposes an excise tax on the consumption of a good. The tax will have the least impact on the market equilibrium quantity for which of the following combinations of the price elasticities of demand and supply? | Absolute Value of Elasticity of Demand | Elasticity of Supply | |----------------------------------------|----------------------| |
unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The tax reduces quantity the least when both demand and supply are inelastic, so the correct answer is E. When both sides are relatively unresponsive to price, neither buyers nor sellers adjust their behavior much, so the equilibrium quantity falls only slightly. Choice D is tempting because inelastic demand means consumers do not cut back much, but elastic supply means producers are very responsive and will reduce output significantly, causing a larger drop in quantity than when both sides are inelastic.

text: The monopsonist’s marginal factor (resource) cost curve for labor is

options.A: above the labor supply curve because the product price is found on the demand curve above where marginal cost equals marginal revenue
options.B: above the labor supply curve because to hire more workers the firm must raise the wage for all workers
options.C: below the labor supply curve because the firm is a wage taker
options.D: below the labor supply curve because of diminishing marginal returns to labor
options.E: below the labor supply curve because to sell additional units of output the firm must lower its product price

explanation: A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve and must increase the wage to attract additional workers, paying that higher wage to everyone already employed. This means the marginal factor cost of hiring one more worker exceeds the wage shown on the supply curve, so the MFC curve lies above it. Choice E is tempting because it describes a product-market monopoly, where marginal revenue lies below demand, but that logic does not apply to a monopsonist's labor cost.

text: Which of the following best demonstrates nonrivalry in consumption?

options.A: Occupying a seat in a sold-out movie theatre
options.B: Sharing rent equally among roommates
options.C: Catching fish in a local pond
options.D: Playing golf on a crowded public golf course
options.E: Listening to a radio program Item 57 was not scored.

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: Nonrivalry means that one person consuming a good does not reduce the amount available for others. Listening to a radio program is nonrival because millions of people can tune in to the same station at the same time without affecting each other. A tempting wrong answer is playing golf on a crowded public course, because the limited space makes it rivalrous—one golfer’s use prevents others from using that same spot.

text: The Lorenz curve is used to study the

options.A: relationship between output and unemployment
options.B: relationship between income and consumption
options.C: extent of income inequality within a society
options.D: incidence of an excise tax on buyers and sellers in a market
options.E: impact of foreign trade on domestic production of goods

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: The Lorenz curve graphs the cumulative percentage of income received by each cumulative percentage of a population, which makes it a tool for measuring income distribution and inequality. The farther the curve sits from the line of perfect equality, the greater the income inequality in that society. Choice B may seem tempting because it involves income, but the relationship between income and consumption is explained by the consumption function, not the Lorenz curve.

text: An effective minimum wage policy in a competitive market will increase unemployment and increase the total earnings of labor only if the demand for labor is

options.A: relatively inelastic
options.B: relatively elastic
options.C: unit elastic
options.D: greater than the supply
options.E: positively related to the wage rate

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government
explanation: If labor demand is relatively inelastic, employers do not reduce employment very much when the wage rises, so the higher minimum wage raises total labor earnings even though some unemployment occurs. If demand were elastic, the drop in jobs would be proportionally larger and total earnings would fall instead. Many students incorrectly choose elastic because they think a strong response helps workers, but a large hiring cut actually reduces overall pay.

text: Compared with a perfectly competitive market, a single-price monopoly with the same market demand and cost curves will

options.A: increase output and price
options.B: increase output and decrease price
options.C: decrease output and price
options.D: decrease output and increase price

explanation: A monopolist produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and because marginal revenue lies below the demand curve, the resulting quantity is lower than the competitive output. The monopolist then sets the price by going up to the demand curve, yielding a higher price than in perfect competition. Choice B is tempting if you assume a larger firm always produces more and charges less, but a monopoly restricts output to raise price and maximize profit.

text: The study of economics exists because people are confronted with the basic problem of

options.A: elasticity
options.B: negative externality
options.C: scarcity
options.D: overabundance
options.E: monopoly

explanation: The entire discipline of economics rests on scarcity, the reality that unlimited human wants face limited resources, forcing societies to make allocation choices. Without scarcity, there would be no need to study trade-offs, costs, or how markets function. Other terms like monopoly or negative externality describe specific market issues, but they are not the root problem that makes economic analysis necessary.

text: The table above shows the total benefit associated with reducing different levels of pollution on a small island. The cost of eliminating one ton of pollution is $150. Which of the following is the optimal quantity of pollution to eliminate?

options.A: 5 tons
options.B: 4 tons
options.C: 3 tons
options.D: 2 tons

unit: Market Failure & the Role of Government

text: If a hurricane reduced the crab population, the price of crabs and quantity sold would change in which of the following ways? Price Quantity

options.A: Increase Increase
options.B: Increase Decrease
options.C: Decrease Increase
options.D: Decrease Decrease
options.E: No change Decrease

explanation: A hurricane that reduces the crab population decreases supply, shifting the supply curve to the left. With demand unchanged, the new equilibrium occurs at a higher price and a lower quantity. Choice A is tempting if you mistakenly think the shock increases demand, but a smaller catch means sellers raise prices while selling fewer crabs.

text: To determine whether two goods are complements, one would calculate the

options.A: price elasticity of demand
options.B: price elasticity of supply
options.C: income elasticity of demand
options.D: cross-price elasticity of demand
options.E: input-price elasticity of supply Quantity of Pollution Reduction (in tons) | Total Benefit (in dollars) ---|--- 0 | 0 1 | 300 2 | 550 3 | 650 4 | 725 5 | 775

explanation: Cross-price elasticity of demand measures how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a price change in another good, and a negative result means the goods are complements. Many students mistakenly choose price elasticity of demand because it involves price and quantity, but it only tracks a single good's own price sensitivity and cannot reveal whether two goods are related.

text: The diagram above depicts the demand and supply curves for good Y. The perfectly competitive market is initially in equilibrium, but the government decides to institute a price floor program by setting the price of good Y at P_F and agrees to purchase all unsold units of good Y from the producers. The cost of this program to the government is represented by which of the following areas?

options.A: 0P_F JQ_2

options.C: GIKH
